title: Ostara Homes Outlook Turns Negative as Sales Slow and Debt Rises
author: Tomas Belwick
body:
Meridian Ratings has revised the outlook on Ostara Homes to negative from stable and affirmed its BBB minus long-term issuer rating. Slower reservations and higher spending on land have increased borrowing. The company builds mid-priced homes in Ostara, Amberford and the outer districts of Saltmarsh.

Net reservations fell 14% in the eight months to August compared with the same period last year. Completed but unsold homes increased to 246 from 171 at December. Net debt reached KRN 392 million, equivalent to 3.7 times operating profit before depreciation over the preceding 12 months.

Cash and undrawn committed facilities total KRN 168 million, against KRN 61 million of debt due within a year. This supports the rating despite weaker trading. Meridian could lower the rating if inventory continues to build or net debt remains above four times operating profit before depreciation for a sustained period.

title: Meridian Rates Saltmarsh Waterworks Bond in Line With Issuer Rating
author: Mara Ternell
body:
Meridian Ratings has assigned an A minus rating to Saltmarsh Waterworks’ proposed KRN 180 million senior unsecured bond. The issue rating matches the company’s long-term issuer rating, which remains A minus with a stable outlook. The bond is expected to mature in September 2033.

The company intends to use KRN 120 million of the proceeds to repay a bank loan due in February 2027. The balance will fund pipe replacement and treatment equipment within its existing investment programme. The transaction would extend debt maturities while leaving total borrowing within Meridian’s previous forecasts.

The proposed bonds will rank equally with the company’s other senior unsecured obligations. Meridian’s assessment assumes that the final terms are consistent with the draft documents reviewed. Cost overruns or a material increase in borrowing beyond the current programme could weaken financial headroom, but neither is included in the base forecast.

title: Meridian Upgrades Kestrel Bay Savings After Stronger Capital and Lower Arrears
author: Elian Voss
body:

title: Meridian Assigns BBB Rating to Amberford Packaging With Stable Outlook
author: Tomas Belwick
body:

Its established customer relationships support earnings, although exposure to pulp prices limits the rating.

The company plans to spend KRN 74 million on a replacement production line over the next year. Meridian expects net debt to remain below 2.8 times operating profit before depreciation. The stable outlook assumes the project stays within budget and customer demand remains broadly consistent with current orders.

title: Kestrian Regional Banks Face Narrower Margins Despite Steady Loan Demand
author: Elian Voss
body:
Meridian Ratings expects profitability at Kestria’s regional banks to weaken modestly during the remainder of 2026 as deposit costs rise. Its review of eight rated lenders found that average net interest margins fell to 2.7% in June from 2.9% in December. The sector outlook remains stable.

Loans grew by 3.6% over the same period, led by small business borrowing in Ostara and residential lending around Saltmarsh. Customer deposits increased by 2.8%. Banks have offered higher rates on fixed-term accounts to retain savers, reducing the benefit of growth in interest income.

Arrears remain manageable, with loans more than 90 days overdue representing 1.8% of the reviewed portfolios. Construction borrowers account for much of the recent increase. Meridian expects lenders to maintain current capital buffers, but banks with concentrated property exposure have less room to absorb unexpected losses.

title: Meridian Ratings Affirms Saltmarsh Waterworks at A Minus With Stable Outlook
author: Mara Ternell
body:
Meridian Ratings has affirmed Saltmarsh Waterworks’ long-term issuer rating at A minus with a stable outlook. The rating reflects steady demand, predictable regulated income and adequate funding for repairs. The company supplies drinking water to 284,000 households and businesses in and around Kestria’s capital.

Revenue reached KRN 418 million in the year to June, up 4.8% from the previous year. Cash generated from operations covered interest payments 5.2 times. Water lost through leaks fell to 18.6% from 20.1%, although older pipes in the eastern districts remain a significant maintenance cost.

The stable outlook assumes annual capital spending of about KRN 110 million and no substantial debt-funded expansion. Available cash and committed borrowing facilities cover debt falling due over the next 18 months. A sustained increase in debt without matching earnings growth could put pressure on the rating.

title: Kestrian Food Producers Maintain Stable Outlook as Input Costs Ease
author: Céline Arvane
body:
Meridian Ratings has maintained a stable outlook for Kestria’s packaged food sector. Lower grain and container costs are helping producers rebuild margins, although household spending remains subdued. Across six rated companies, average operating margins increased to 11.2% in the first half of 2026 from 10.4% a year earlier.

Sales volumes rose just 0.8%, with stronger demand for basic products offset by weaker purchases of premium lines. Producers supplying retailers in Saltmarsh and Amberford reported increased use of promotions. Meridian expects price competition to limit how much of the recent cost relief companies retain.

The sector’s median net debt stood at 2.4 times operating profit before depreciation at June. Most rated producers have sufficient cash and committed facilities for planned investment over the next year. Debt-funded acquisitions or prolonged discounting would create greater pressure than the modest volume growth currently assumed in Meridian’s forecasts.

title: Meridian Places Bracken Freight Under Review Following Proposed Harbour Acquisition
author: Tomas Belwick
body:
Meridian Ratings has placed Bracken Freight’s BBB long-term issuer rating under review for downgrade after the company announced an agreement to acquire Kestrel Bay Harbour Services. The proposed KRN 460 million purchase would expand Bracken’s storage and cargo handling operations but could materially increase debt.

Bracken has disclosed a committed bridge loan covering the full purchase price. It is also considering an equity issue, although the amount and timing have not been confirmed. Based on debt-only funding, Meridian estimates that net debt could exceed four times annual operating profit before depreciation immediately after completion.

The review will examine the final funding mix, integration costs and the acquired business’s cash generation. Bracken expects completion before the end of October, subject to the remaining transaction conditions. Meridian will resolve the review once it has sufficient evidence to assess the combined company’s financial position.

title: Val-Brume Heating Retains BBB Plus Rating Ahead of Winter Demand
author: Céline Arvane
body:
Meridian Ratings has affirmed Val-Brume Heating’s BBB plus long-term issuer rating with a stable outlook. The company provides district heating to 42,000 properties in Kestria’s French-speaking region. Its established network and contracted customer base support the rating, while seasonal cash needs and fuel costs remain constraints.

Fuel stocks at the end of September covered approximately 11 weeks of expected winter consumption. Fixed-price supply contracts cover 76% of forecast purchases through March 2027. The company also has an undrawn KRN 65 million revolving facility available to meet short-term working capital requirements.

Meridian expects operating cash flow to cover interest payments at least four times over the coming year. The forecast allows for routine maintenance and a KRN 28 million boiler replacement. An unusually prolonged cold period would increase purchases, but existing liquidity provides a reasonable buffer against that pressure.

title: Ostara Homes Outlook Turns Negative as Sales Slow and Debt Rises
author: Tomas Belwick
body:
Meridian Ratings has revised the outlook on Ostara Homes to negative from stable and affirmed its BBB minus long-term issuer rating. Slower reservations and higher spending on land have increased borrowing. The company builds mid-priced homes in Ostara, Amberford and the outer districts of Saltmarsh.

Net reservations fell 14% in the eight months to August compared with the same period last year. Completed but unsold homes increased to 246 from 171 at December. Net debt reached KRN 392 million, equivalent to 3.7 times operating profit before depreciation over the preceding 12 months.

Cash and undrawn committed facilities total KRN 168 million, against KRN 61 million of debt due within a year. This supports the rating despite weaker trading. Meridian could lower the rating if inventory continues to build or net debt remains above four times operating profit before depreciation for a sustained period.

title: Meridian Rates Saltmarsh Waterworks Bond in Line With Issuer Rating
author: Mara Ternell
body:
Meridian Ratings has assigned an A minus rating to Saltmarsh Waterworks’ proposed KRN 180 million senior unsecured bond. The issue rating matches the company’s long-term issuer rating, which remains A minus with a stable outlook. The bond is expected to mature in September 2033.

The company intends to use KRN 120 million of the proceeds to repay a bank loan due in February 2027. The balance will fund pipe replacement and treatment equipment within its existing investment programme. The transaction would extend debt maturities while leaving total borrowing within Meridian’s previous forecasts.

The proposed bonds will rank equally with the company’s other senior unsecured obligations. Meridian’s assessment assumes that the final terms are consistent with the draft documents reviewed. Cost overruns or a material increase in borrowing beyond the current programme could weaken financial headroom, but neither is included in the base forecast.

title: Amberford Packaging Reports Production Delay but Retains Financial Headroom
author: Tomas Belwick
body:
Meridian Ratings says a delay to Amberford Packaging’s replacement production line does not currently affect its BBB issuer rating or stable outlook. The company now expects commissioning in February 2027, two months later than planned, following a fault identified during equipment testing at the supplier’s workshop.

The project budget has risen to KRN 81 million from KRN 74 million. Amberford expects to keep its existing line operating until the replacement is ready, allowing it to fulfil contracted orders. The delay will defer expected efficiency savings and add approximately KRN 3 million in temporary maintenance costs.

Meridian’s revised forecast puts peak net debt at 2.9 times operating profit before depreciation, compared with less than 2.8 times previously. Existing liquidity can absorb the additional spending. Further delays, lost orders or substantially higher costs could reduce the headroom supporting the stable outlook and prompt a rating review.

title: Meridian Publishes Updated Criteria for Rating Kestrian District Heating Providers
author: Mara Ternell
body:
Meridian Ratings has published updated criteria for assessing district heating providers in Kestria. The criteria take effect today and apply to new ratings and future reviews. They give more detailed guidance on fuel procurement, seasonal liquidity and the financial effect of delays in recovering costs through customer tariffs.

The update follows a consultation that closed on 18 September. Meridian received nine written responses from rated companies, investors and other market participants. The final text clarifies how analysts assess committed credit facilities and distinguishes fuel already held in storage from purchases covered by future supply contracts.

Meridian has assessed its existing district heating ratings against the revised criteria and identified no immediate rating changes. The update does not alter the rating or outlook on Val-Brume Heating affirmed on 5 October. Individual reviews will continue to consider network condition, customer concentration and each provider’s ability to absorb unexpected costs.

title: Meridian Downgrades Ostara Homes as Cancellations Increase and Liquidity Weakens
author: Céline Arvane
body:
Meridian Ratings has downgraded Ostara Homes’ long-term issuer rating to BB plus from BBB minus. The outlook is negative. The downgrade follows a sharp increase in cancellations and a reduction in available borrowing facilities, which weaken the company’s ability to carry its growing stock of unsold homes.

Figures supplied on 21 October show that completed but unsold homes reached 289 at September, compared with 246 at August. Cancellations accounted for 27% of gross reservations during September. Cash and undrawn committed facilities fell to KRN 112 million after a lender declined to renew a KRN 40 million facility.

Ostara Homes has suspended new land purchases and plans selective discounts to release cash from finished properties. These steps should help liquidity, but lower selling prices will put further pressure on earnings. Meridian could lower the rating again if available funding falls materially or sales fail to cover construction spending and scheduled debt payments.

title: Meridian Confirms Bracken Freight Rating After Equity Funding Reduces Acquisition Debt
author: Tomas Belwick
body:
Meridian Ratings has confirmed Bracken Freight’s BBB long-term issuer rating with a stable outlook and removed it from review for downgrade. The action follows completion of its KRN 460 million acquisition of Kestrel Bay Harbour Services and confirmation of a larger equity contribution than previously disclosed.

Bracken raised KRN 250 million through an equity issue completed on 19 October and funded the remaining purchase price through its bridge facility. The acquisition completed today. Meridian estimates opening net debt at 2.8 times combined annual operating profit before depreciation, materially below the debt-only case considered on 8 October.

The stable outlook allows for KRN 22 million of integration spending over the next 12 months and assumes no further large acquisitions. Bracken plans to replace the bridge borrowing with longer-term funding within six months. Delayed refinancing or weaker cargo volumes could reduce rating headroom, although current cash generation supports the confirmed rating.

title: Meridian Affirms Fenmere Commercial Bank as Property Lending Remains Concentrated
author: Elian Voss
body:
Meridian Ratings has affirmed Fenmere Commercial Bank’s BBB long-term issuer rating with a stable outlook. The Saltmarsh-based lender benefits from steady business deposits and adequate capital. Its relatively large exposure to commercial property continues to constrain the rating, particularly lending secured on smaller office buildings.

Commercial property represented 31% of gross loans at the end of September, down from 34% a year earlier. Loans more than 90 days overdue rose to 2.5% from 2.1% over that period. Additional provisions reduced nine-month profit to KRN 47 million, 12% below the comparable period.

The bank’s core capital ratio of 14.2% provides capacity to absorb further losses within Meridian’s base forecast. Deposits increased by 3.1% during the first nine months, supporting liquidity. The stable outlook assumes gradual reductions in property concentration and no sharp deterioration among the bank’s largest borrowers.

title: Val-Brume Packaging Downgraded to BB+ Following Weaker Cash Generation
author: Elise Dorne and Dario Selven
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has lowered Val-Brume Packaging's senior unsecured bond rating to BB+ from BBB-. The outlook is stable. The producer of cartons and food containers has reported weaker earnings and a larger working capital requirement than Northstar assumed in its previous review.

Operating profit before depreciation fell 22% to KRN 41 million in the year ended July, while debt increased to KRN 205 million. Higher paper input costs and slower customer payments contributed to the deterioration. Debt reached 5.0 times operating profit, compared with 3.6 times a year earlier. The company serves food producers across Kestria from its principal factory in Val-Brume.

Cash of KRN 19 million and an undrawn committed facility of KRN 35 million provide adequate near-term funding. No bond principal is due before 2029. The stable outlook assumes tighter stock control and lower investment spending prevent further debt growth. Another downgrade could follow if cash generation remains negative or available funding falls materially.

title: Amberford Water Receives A- Rating for Network Renewal Bond
author: Mara Vellin and Céline Maret
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has assigned an A- rating to Amberford Water's proposed KRN 230 million senior unsecured bond, with a stable outlook. The company plans to use KRN 150 million to repay existing debt and the remainder to replace ageing mains and pumping equipment. The rating is subject to final documents matching the terms reviewed.

Amberford Water supplies 340,000 households and businesses under a licence that links permitted revenue to operating costs and approved investment. Collections remained strong at 98.6% of billed revenue in the year ended June. Water losses declined to 17.2% from 19.1% following repairs to several older sections of the network.

Northstar expects debt to remain close to 4.0 times annual operating profit before depreciation during the renewal programme. The stable outlook assumes spending stays within the approved budget and service performance supports timely cost recovery. Persistent overspending or debt above 4.8 times operating profit could put downward pressure on the rating.

title: Northstar Opens Consultation on Proposed Corporate Liquidity Assessment Changes
author: Nalin Verdan and Dario Selven
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has opened a consultation on proposed changes to its corporate liquidity methodology. The draft explains how analysts would assess seasonal cash needs, restrictions on moving cash between subsidiaries and borrowing facilities that depend on financial conditions. Written responses are invited until 2 October.

The proposal would require a separate assessment of the weakest three-month cash position within the following year. Current analysis places greater emphasis on the full twelve-month period. The draft also clarifies that an uncommitted overdraft would not count as an assured funding source, even when an issuer has used it regularly.

An initial review of 24 rated Kestrian corporate groups suggests that five could receive weaker liquidity assessments under the draft. This would not automatically change their ratings, which also reflect business strength and debt levels. The existing methodology remains in force during consultation. Northstar will publish its conclusions after reviewing responses and completing further testing.

title: Estuary Freight Outlook Turns Negative as Bond Refinancing Remains Unresolved
author: Tomas Arven and Céline Maret
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has affirmed Estuary Freight's BBB- senior unsecured bond rating and revised the outlook to negative from stable. The Kestrel Bay cargo handler has KRN 160 million of bonds falling due in February 2027. Discussions with lenders are continuing, but the company has not secured replacement funding.

At 31 July, Estuary Freight held KRN 38 million in unrestricted cash and had KRN 25 million available under committed facilities. Cargo volumes fell 6% in the first seven months of the year, mainly because of lower building material shipments. Northstar estimates debt at 4.4 times annual operating profit before depreciation, against 3.8 times at the end of 2025.

The negative outlook reflects the narrowing time available to refinance. Northstar could lower the rating if funding arrangements remain incomplete or operating performance weakens further. A return to a stable outlook would require sufficient committed funding to repay the bonds and evidence that cargo earnings have steadied.

title: Kestrian Food Producers Face Narrower Margins as Packaging Costs Rise
author: Elise Dorne and Nalin Verdan
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has revised its outlook for Kestrian packaged food producers to negative from stable. The change reflects higher packaging and distribution costs, together with limited scope to raise selling prices. It is a sector assessment and does not change any individual bond rating.

Across the agency's sample of seven fictional issuers, packaging costs increased by an average of 11% in the first half of 2026, while selling prices rose 3%. Northstar expects the sample's operating margin before depreciation to fall to roughly 9% this year from 10.4% in 2025. Smaller producers supplying shops around Ostara have less purchasing power and face the greatest pressure.

Most rated producers retain adequate cash reserves and have no large bond repayments within twelve months. This should limit immediate rating pressure. The agency will focus on stock levels, customer payment times and whether cost savings protect cash generation. Companies that borrow to fund dividends while margins weaken could face individual rating reviews.

title: Northstar Affirms Bracken Grid Bonds at BBB with Stable Outlook
author: Mara Vellin and Tomas Arven
body:
SALTMarsh — Northstar Credit Analytics has affirmed its BBB rating on Bracken Grid's KRN 420 million senior unsecured bonds. The outlook remains stable. The electricity network operator serves 610,000 connections across Amberford and surrounding districts. Its regulated network income provides a predictable source of cash, although a substantial maintenance programme limits room for additional borrowing.

For the six months ended 30 June, revenue rose 4.2% to KRN 286 million and operating profit before depreciation reached KRN 112 million. Debt stood at 3.7 times annualised operating profit, compared with 3.9 times at December. Available cash and committed borrowing facilities covered the company's next twelve months of scheduled debt payments.

The stable outlook assumes annual capital spending of about KRN 95 million and no material acquisition. Northstar could lower the rating if debt remained above 4.5 times operating profit or network penalties materially reduced cash generation. A higher rating would require sustained debt reduction alongside reliable service performance.

title: Bracken Grid Bond Rating Holds After Amberford Storm Disruption
author: Tomas Arven and Mara Vellin
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has maintained Bracken Grid's BBB senior unsecured bond rating and stable outlook following the 6 October storm in the Amberford district. The storm damaged overhead lines and interrupted supplies to 74,000 connections. By the evening of 8 October, the company had restored power to all but 1,900 affected connections.

Bracken Grid's preliminary estimate places repair costs at KRN 18 million to KRN 24 million. Northstar has assumed the full upper estimate in its initial assessment without relying on insurance receipts. The company had KRN 72 million in cash and KRN 110 million of undrawn committed facilities at the end of September.

These resources should allow repairs to proceed without materially weakening liquidity. The rating also allows for occasional weather-related disruption. Northstar will review the final repair bill, compensation payments and any changes to planned maintenance. Costs substantially above the current estimate, or evidence of wider network weaknesses, could alter the assessment.

title: Ostara Rental Housing Outlook Remains Stable Despite Higher Maintenance Spending
author: Mara Vellin and Dario Selven
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has maintained a stable sector outlook for rated rental housing companies operating in Ostara. High occupancy and steady rent collection continue to support earnings, although repairs and borrowing costs are absorbing more cash. The assessment covers four issuers with a combined 28,400 homes.

title: Corporate Liquidity Consultation Closes with Twelve Responses Under Review
author: Nalin Verdan and Céline Maret
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics received twelve responses to its proposed corporate liquidity methodology changes before the consultation closed on 2 October. Submissions came from rated companies, bond investors and lending firms. Analysts are reviewing the comments alongside additional testing of the proposed three-month cash assessment.

Several respondents supported clearer treatment of restricted cash and uncommitted borrowing. Others asked how the agency would assess seasonal businesses whose lowest cash balance occurs shortly before a predictable collection period. Northstar will consider these points before deciding whether to adopt the changes. No rating or liquidity assessment has changed as a result of the consultation, and the existing methodology remains applicable. The agency plans to publish a summary of the main comments with its final decision. Confidential financial information supplied by respondents will be excluded from that summary.

title: Val-Brume Packaging Downgraded to BB+ Following Weaker Cash Generation
author: Elise Dorne and Dario Selven
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has lowered Val-Brume Packaging's senior unsecured bond rating to BB+ from BBB-. The outlook is stable. The producer of cartons and food containers has reported weaker earnings and a larger working capital requirement than Northstar assumed in its previous review.

Operating profit before depreciation fell 22% to KRN 41 million in the year ended July, while debt increased to KRN 205 million. Higher paper input costs and slower customer payments contributed to the deterioration. Debt reached 5.0 times operating profit, compared with 3.6 times a year earlier. The company serves food producers across Kestria from its principal factory in Val-Brume.

Cash of KRN 19 million and an undrawn committed facility of KRN 35 million provide adequate near-term funding. No bond principal is due before 2029. The stable outlook assumes tighter stock control and lower investment spending prevent further debt growth. Another downgrade could follow if cash generation remains negative or available funding falls materially.

title: Amberford Water Receives A- Rating for Network Renewal Bond
author: Mara Vellin and Céline Maret
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has assigned an A- rating to Amberford Water's proposed KRN 230 million senior unsecured bond, with a stable outlook. The company plans to use KRN 150 million to repay existing debt and the remainder to replace ageing mains and pumping equipment. The rating is subject to final documents matching the terms reviewed.

Amberford Water supplies 340,000 households and businesses under a licence that links permitted revenue to operating costs and approved investment. Collections remained strong at 98.6% of billed revenue in the year ended June. Water losses declined to 17.2% from 19.1% following repairs to several older sections of the network.

Northstar expects debt to remain close to 4.0 times annual operating profit before depreciation during the renewal programme. The stable outlook assumes spending stays within the approved budget and service performance supports timely cost recovery. Persistent overspending or debt above 4.8 times operating profit could put downward pressure on the rating.

title: Northstar Opens Consultation on Proposed Corporate Liquidity Assessment Changes
author: Nalin Verdan and Dario Selven
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has opened a consultation on proposed changes to its corporate liquidity methodology. The draft explains how analysts would assess seasonal cash needs, restrictions on moving cash between subsidiaries and borrowing facilities that depend on financial conditions. Written responses are invited until 2 October.

The proposal would require a separate assessment of the weakest three-month cash position within the following year. Current analysis places greater emphasis on the full twelve-month period. The draft also clarifies that an uncommitted overdraft would not count as an assured funding source, even when an issuer has used it regularly.

An initial review of 24 rated Kestrian corporate groups suggests that five could receive weaker liquidity assessments under the draft. This would not automatically change their ratings, which also reflect business strength and debt levels. The existing methodology remains in force during consultation. Northstar will publish its conclusions after reviewing responses and completing further testing.

title: Estuary Freight Outlook Turns Negative as Bond Refinancing Remains Unresolved
author: Tomas Arven and Céline Maret
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has affirmed Estuary Freight's BBB- senior unsecured bond rating and revised the outlook to negative from stable. The Kestrel Bay cargo handler has KRN 160 million of bonds falling due in February 2027. Discussions with lenders are continuing, but the company has not secured replacement funding.

At 31 July, Estuary Freight held KRN 38 million in unrestricted cash and had KRN 25 million available under committed facilities. Cargo volumes fell 6% in the first seven months of the year, mainly because of lower building material shipments. Northstar estimates debt at 4.4 times annual operating profit before depreciation, against 3.8 times at the end of 2025.

The negative outlook reflects the narrowing time available to refinance. Northstar could lower the rating if funding arrangements remain incomplete or operating performance weakens further. A return to a stable outlook would require sufficient committed funding to repay the bonds and evidence that cargo earnings have steadied.

title: Kestrian Food Producers Face Narrower Margins as Packaging Costs Rise
author: Elise Dorne and Nalin Verdan
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has revised its outlook for Kestrian packaged food producers to negative from stable. The change reflects higher packaging and distribution costs, together with limited scope to raise selling prices. It is a sector assessment and does not change any individual bond rating.

Across the agency's sample of seven fictional issuers, packaging costs increased by an average of 11% in the first half of 2026, while selling prices rose 3%. Northstar expects the sample's operating margin before depreciation to fall to roughly 9% this year from 10.4% in 2025. Smaller producers supplying shops around Ostara have less purchasing power and face the greatest pressure.

Most rated producers retain adequate cash reserves and have no large bond repayments within twelve months. This should limit immediate rating pressure. The agency will focus on stock levels, customer payment times and whether cost savings protect cash generation. Companies that borrow to fund dividends while margins weaken could face individual rating reviews.

title: Estuary Freight Downgraded to BB as Refinancing Options Narrow
author: Tomas Arven and Dario Selven
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has lowered Estuary Freight's senior unsecured bond rating to BB from BBB- and concluded the review opened on 13 October. The outlook is negative. Further information supplied during the review shows that the company has limited readily available funding for its KRN 160 million February 2027 bond repayment.

Of the KRN 25 million previously reported as available under committed facilities, KRN 15 million expires in January 2027. Northstar therefore excludes that amount when assessing resources for the bond maturity. The proposed storage yard sale remains at an early stage, with no agreed buyer or binding timetable. September cargo earnings also fell below management's revised budget.

The downgrade principally reflects weaker refinancing prospects and reduced financial flexibility. The revised liquidity methodology published yesterday also informs the assessment of facility availability. The negative outlook indicates further downside if replacement funding remains unsecured. A stable outlook would require a credible, committed repayment plan and enough cash to continue ordinary operations.

title: Northstar Adopts Revised Liquidity Methodology with Seasonal Cash Guidance
author: Nalin Verdan and Céline Maret
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has published its revised corporate liquidity methodology, effective today. The final document adds a review of the weakest three-month cash position within the following year and clarifies how analysts treat restricted cash, uncommitted borrowing and conditions attached to committed facilities.

Following consultation, the agency has added worked examples for seasonal businesses. Analysts may recognise expected customer receipts when supported by a consistent collection record, but must also test a reasonable delay. Cash held by a subsidiary will count only where it can legally and practically meet the obligations being assessed.

Northstar has also published an anonymised summary of the twelve consultation responses. It will apply the revised methodology to existing corporate ratings over the next three months and to new assignments immediately. Publication itself changes no ratings. Any resulting action will receive a separate release explaining the issuer's circumstances and the role of the revised assessment.

title: Estuary Freight Placed Under Review After Refinancing Talks End
author: Tomas Arven and Nalin Verdan
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has placed Estuary Freight's BBB- senior unsecured bond rating under review for downgrade. The action follows the end of negotiations with a proposed lead lender without a refinancing agreement. The company's KRN 160 million bond remains due in February 2027.

Estuary Freight informed Northstar that it is approaching other lenders and considering the sale of a storage yard near Kestrel Bay. Neither option currently provides committed funds. Unrestricted cash was KRN 31 million at 30 September, down from KRN 38 million at 31 July. Available committed borrowing remained KRN 25 million, and trading continued below the agency's earlier expectations.

The review will focus on the size, timing and conditions of alternative funding. Northstar expects to resolve it once sufficient information is available and may lower the rating by more than one grade. A property valuation or an expression of lender interest alone would not establish that the February repayment can be met.

title: Bracken Grid Bond Rating Holds After Amberford Storm Disruption
author: Tomas Arven and Mara Vellin
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has maintained Bracken Grid's BBB senior unsecured bond rating and stable outlook following the 6 October storm in the Amberford district. The storm damaged overhead lines and interrupted supplies to 74,000 connections. By the evening of 8 October, the company had restored power to all but 1,900 affected connections.

Bracken Grid's preliminary estimate places repair costs at KRN 18 million to KRN 24 million. Northstar has assumed the full upper estimate in its initial assessment without relying on insurance receipts. The company had KRN 72 million in cash and KRN 110 million of undrawn committed facilities at the end of September.

These resources should allow repairs to proceed without materially weakening liquidity. The rating also allows for occasional weather-related disruption. Northstar will review the final repair bill, compensation payments and any changes to planned maintenance. Costs substantially above the current estimate, or evidence of wider network weaknesses, could alter the assessment.

title: Val-Brume Packaging Rating Affirmed After Investment Spending Is Reduced
author: Céline Maret and Dario Selven
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has affirmed Val-Brume Packaging's BB+ senior unsecured bond rating and stable outlook after the company reduced its investment budget. Management has deferred a second printing line, cutting planned spending for the current financial year to KRN 18 million from KRN 34 million.

The decision preserves cash while the company addresses the working capital pressures behind its September downgrade. Unrestricted cash stood at KRN 22 million at the end of September, with KRN 35 million still available under its committed facility. Early collections from overdue customers helped the improvement, although one month of stronger receipts does not establish a sustained recovery.

Northstar continues to expect debt near 5.0 times annual operating profit before depreciation in the near term. The revised liquidity assessment supports the existing rating because available resources cover projected seasonal needs. An upgrade would require durable earnings recovery and lower debt. Renewed cash outflows, weaker facility access or substantial additional borrowing could lead to another downgrade.

title: Kestrian Retail Bond Issuers Enter Winter with Uneven Cash Buffers
author: Elise Dorne and Nalin Verdan
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has maintained a negative outlook for Kestrian discretionary retailers in its latest sector review. Households are limiting larger purchases, while retailers have already paid for much of their winter stock. The agency expects differences in cash reserves to matter more than modest changes in reported sales.

Among six rated issuers, stock values at the end of September were 9% higher than a year earlier, while sales for the preceding three months rose only 1%. Two chains operating mainly in Saltmarsh and Kestrel Bay increased promotional discounts to clear older goods. Across the sample, average operating margins before depreciation fell to 6.2% from 7.1%.

Four issuers have committed facilities extending beyond their seasonal borrowing peak. The remaining two rely more heavily on cash generated during winter trading. Northstar is testing slower stock sales and delayed supplier credit separately for each company. The sector outlook does not imply that every retailer will be downgraded, and no individual rating changes accompany this report.

title: Coppermere Components Upgraded to BBB After Sustained Debt Reduction
author: Elise Dorne and Mara Vellin
body:
Northstar Credit Analytics has raised Coppermere Components' senior unsecured bond rating to BBB from BBB-, with a stable outlook. The Amberford manufacturer supplies replacement parts for industrial pumps and ventilation equipment. The upgrade reflects sustained debt reduction, a broader customer base and improved cash collection.

Debt fell to KRN 126 million at the end of August from KRN 171 million eighteen months earlier. Over the same period, debt relative to annual operating profit before depreciation declined from 3.8 times to 2.6 times. The largest customer now accounts for 14% of revenue, compared with 23% two years ago. Replacement orders provide more consistent demand than sales tied to new construction.

Cash and committed facilities comfortably cover the company's lowest projected three-month funding position under Northstar's revised methodology. The stable outlook assumes moderate investment and no large debt-funded acquisition. A downgrade could follow if debt rises above 3.5 times operating profit for a sustained period or customer concentration increases materially.

title: Equipment programme expands after strong demand from regional manufacturers
author: Devran Holt
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank has increased its equipment lending programme from KRN 40 million to KRN 60 million. Since applications opened on 24 August, the bank has approved KRN 26.4 million across 19 facilities. Of that amount, KRN 11.8 million has been drawn by borrowers.

Companies in Amberford and Ostara account for just over half the approved lending by value. Purchases include cutting machines, temperature-controlled storage and packing lines. Approval totals represent agreed facilities rather than equipment already installed, and borrowers draw funds as supplier invoices become due.

The additional allocation is available to new applications from today. Loan sizes remain between KRN 250,000 and KRN 4 million, with terms of three to seven years. Each application will receive a separate credit assessment. Businesses should obtain approval before relying on bank funding to place a binding equipment order.

title: Business reference rate falls by a further quarter point
author: Mara Ellery
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank will lower its business reference rate from 6.25% to 6.00% on 21 September. Borrowers whose agreements track this rate will receive the reduction automatically. The change follows the quarter-point reduction that took effect on 24 August.

Together, the two changes reduce annual interest by KRN 5,000 on an unchanged KRN 1 million balance, before any fees and subject to the terms of the agreement. Fixed-rate borrowing is unaffected. Loans linked to a different reference rate will continue to follow the calculation set out in their contracts.

The bank reviewed its funding costs and lending commitments before making the decision. Updated repayment information will be sent where monthly payments change. Customers with interest-only facilities will see the new rate applied to the relevant days in their next interest calculation and can request a breakdown from their relationship team.

title: Val-Brume lending desk adds appointments for French-speaking businesses
author: Tomas Arlen
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank has added twelve weekly appointments at its Val-Brume lending desk for businesses that prefer to discuss borrowing in French. The additional sessions are available on Tuesdays and Thursdays and can be held at the branch or by telephone.

Appointments cover working capital, equipment purchases and reviews of existing facilities. Businesses can request a document checklist in French before their meeting. The desk will also help customers identify which financial records are needed, although it cannot prepare accounts or provide independent legal advice.

There is no appointment charge and no obligation to apply for a loan. Lending decisions remain subject to the bank’s usual affordability and security checks. The expansion follows a six-week booking review in which the Val-Brume team recorded an average wait of nine working days for a French-language lending appointment.

title: Bank publishes revised fees for business lending administration
author: Leonie Venn
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank has published a revised schedule of business lending administration fees, taking effect on 5 October. The fee for a borrower-requested security amendment will fall from KRN 450 to KRN 325. Providing a duplicate annual interest certificate will become free, replacing the current KRN 35 charge.

The fee for reviewing a request to extend an overdraft temporarily will rise from KRN 175 to KRN 225. It covers the review and does not guarantee approval. Customers will be told whether a charge applies before they ask the bank to proceed with any chargeable work.

The changes do not alter agreed loan margins or repayment dates. Where an existing agreement fixes an administration fee, that agreement will continue to apply. The full schedule is available from relationship teams and on the bank’s website, with copies in French available for customers in Val-Brume.

title: New equipment lending programme opens with forty million crowns
author: Devran Holt
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank today opened a KRN 40 million lending programme for mid-sized companies replacing production equipment. Businesses across Kestria can apply for loans of between KRN 250,000 and KRN 4 million, with repayment terms of three to seven years.

Eligible purchases include workshop machinery, commercial refrigeration and equipment used to sort or pack goods. Applicants must provide equipment quotations, their latest accounts and a cash-flow forecast. The bank will assess whether repayments remain affordable during quieter trading periods. Purchased equipment will normally form part of the security.

Both existing customers and companies new to the bank may apply. Interest rates and arrangement fees will be set for each borrower and disclosed before an agreement is signed. Applications are open through the bank’s lending teams, including its industrial business desks in Amberford and Kestrel Bay.

title: Harrow & Finch Bank lowers its business reference rate
author: Mara Ellery
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank will reduce its business reference rate from 6.50% to 6.25% on 24 August. The change applies to lending agreements that track the bank’s reference rate. Fixed-rate loans will keep their agreed rates until the end of their fixed terms.

A company with a KRN 2 million loan priced at the reference rate plus 2 percentage points would pay around KRN 417 less interest over a full month, assuming its balance stays unchanged. Actual savings will depend on the number of days in the interest period and the outstanding balance.

The bank is sending notices to affected borrowers this week. Customers do not need to submit a request to receive the reduction. Relationship teams in Saltmarsh, Kestrel Bay, Ostara, Amberford and Val-Brume can explain how the change will appear on individual statements.

title: Ostara businesses offered working capital review appointments this month
author: Tomas Arlen
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank is offering 30 working capital review appointments for mid-sized businesses at its Ostara branch between 12 and 30 October. The sessions are intended for companies preparing for seasonal changes in stock purchases, customer payments or supplier bills.

Each appointment lasts up to an hour and carries no charge. Businesses should bring a thirteen-week cash-flow forecast, a list of unpaid customer invoices and details of existing borrowing. A relationship manager will discuss the timing of expected receipts and payments and identify any information needed for a lending application.

Attendance does not require a company to move its banking arrangements. Any subsequent request for an overdraft or loan will be assessed separately, with rates and fees explained before acceptance. Telephone appointments are available for businesses outside Ostara that cannot attend the branch during the scheduled period.

title: Revised administration fees take effect for business borrowers today
author: Leonie Venn
body:
The business lending administration fees announced by Harrow & Finch Bank on 2 September take effect today. A borrower-requested security amendment now costs KRN 325, down from KRN 450. Duplicate annual interest certificates are now free, removing the previous KRN 35 charge.

Reviewing a request for a temporary overdraft extension now costs KRN 225, an increase of KRN 50. The review fee does not depend on whether the request is approved. Staff must explain the applicable fee and obtain the customer’s agreement before starting a chargeable review.

Requests accepted before today will be charged under the previous schedule. Existing contracts that specify a fixed administration fee retain that fee. Customers can obtain the current schedule from any lending team or download it from the bank’s website. A French-language version is also available through the Val-Brume desk.

Applicants must provide equipment quotations, their latest accounts and a cash-flow forecast. The bank will assess whether repayments remain affordable during quieter trading periods. Purchased equipment will normally form part of the security.

Both existing customers and companies new to the bank may apply. Interest rates and arrangement fees will be set for each borrower and disclosed before an agreement is signed. Applications are open through the bank’s lending teams, including its industrial business desks in Amberford and Kestrel Bay.

title: Harrow & Finch Bank lowers its business reference rate
author: Mara Ellery
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank will reduce its business reference rate from 6.50% to 6.25% on 24 August. The change applies to lending agreements that track the bank’s reference rate. Fixed-rate loans will keep their agreed rates until the end of their fixed terms.

A company with a KRN 2 million loan priced at the reference rate plus 2 percentage points would pay around KRN 417 less interest over a full month, assuming its balance stays unchanged. Actual savings will depend on the number of days in the interest period and the outstanding balance.

The bank is sending notices to affected borrowers this week. Customers do not need to submit a request to receive the reduction. Relationship teams in Saltmarsh, Kestrel Bay, Ostara, Amberford and Val-Brume can explain how the change will appear on individual statements.

title: Kestrel Bay lending team moves to larger customer premises
author: Tomas Arlen
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank’s Kestrel Bay lending team will move to 18 Lantern Quay on 19 October. The new premises provide four private meeting rooms, compared with two at the current office, and a ground-floor entrance with step-free access from the pavement.

The office will serve mid-sized companies seeking lending advice and support with existing facilities. Customer telephone numbers and relationship managers will remain the same. Meetings already booked for 19 October onwards will take place at Lantern Quay, and the bank is contacting customers individually with directions.

The current office at 7 Tern Passage closes to visitors at 16:00 today. Telephone support will remain available during normal opening hours throughout the move. The new office opens at 09:00 on 19 October. It is an appointment-based lending office and does not provide cash deposits, withdrawals or counter payment services.

title: Bank introduces clearer monthly statements for variable-rate business loans
author: Leonie Venn
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank has introduced a revised monthly statement layout for variable-rate business loans. Statements issued from today show the reference rate, the borrower’s agreed margin and the number of days charged at each rate in a single interest table.

Where a rate changes during the statement period, separate rows show the balance and calculation for each part of that period. This will help borrowers check interest following the bank’s reference rate reductions in August and September. Fees will continue to appear separately from interest.

The layout changes how information is presented and does not alter loan terms or payment dates. It was tested with 24 business customers from Saltmarsh, Amberford and Val-Brume. Large-print statements and an explanation in French are available on request. Customers who need help checking a calculation can contact the lending team named on their statement.

title: Ostara businesses offered working capital review appointments this month
author: Tomas Arlen
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank is offering 30 working capital review appointments for mid-sized businesses at its Ostara branch between 12 and 30 October. The sessions are intended for companies preparing for seasonal changes in stock purchases, customer payments or supplier bills.

Each appointment lasts up to an hour and carries no charge. Businesses should bring a thirteen-week cash-flow forecast, a list of unpaid customer invoices and details of existing borrowing. A relationship manager will discuss the timing of expected receipts and payments and identify any information needed for a lending application.

Attendance does not require a company to move its banking arrangements. Any subsequent request for an overdraft or loan will be assessed separately, with rates and fees explained before acceptance. Telephone appointments are available for businesses outside Ostara that cannot attend the branch during the scheduled period.

title: Revised administration fees take effect for business borrowers today
author: Leonie Venn
body:
The business lending administration fees announced by Harrow & Finch Bank on 2 September take effect today. A borrower-requested security amendment now costs KRN 325, down from KRN 450. Duplicate annual interest certificates are now free, removing the previous KRN 35 charge.

Reviewing a request for a temporary overdraft extension now costs KRN 225, an increase of KRN 50. The review fee does not depend on whether the request is approved. Staff must explain the applicable fee and obtain the customer’s agreement before starting a chargeable review.

Requests accepted before today will be charged under the previous schedule. Existing contracts that specify a fixed administration fee retain that fee. Customers can obtain the current schedule from any lending team or download it from the bank’s website. A French-language version is also available through the Val-Brume desk.

title: Equipment programme expands after strong demand from regional manufacturers
author: Devran Holt
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank has increased its equipment lending programme from KRN 40 million to KRN 60 million. Since applications opened on 24 August, the bank has approved KRN 26.4 million across 19 facilities. Of that amount, KRN 11.8 million has been drawn by borrowers.

Companies in Amberford and Ostara account for just over half the approved lending by value. Purchases include cutting machines, temperature-controlled storage and packing lines. Approval totals represent agreed facilities rather than equipment already installed, and borrowers draw funds as supplier invoices become due.

The additional allocation is available to new applications from today. Loan sizes remain between KRN 250,000 and KRN 4 million, with terms of three to seven years. Each application will receive a separate credit assessment. Businesses should obtain approval before relying on bank funding to place a binding equipment order.

title: Business reference rate falls by a further quarter point
author: Mara Ellery
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank will lower its business reference rate from 6.25% to 6.00% on 21 September. Borrowers whose agreements track this rate will receive the reduction automatically. The change follows the quarter-point reduction that took effect on 24 August.

Together, the two changes reduce annual interest by KRN 5,000 on an unchanged KRN 1 million balance, before any fees and subject to the terms of the agreement. Fixed-rate borrowing is unaffected. Loans linked to a different reference rate will continue to follow the calculation set out in their contracts.

The bank reviewed its funding costs and lending commitments before making the decision. Updated repayment information will be sent where monthly payments change. Customers with interest-only facilities will see the new rate applied to the relevant days in their next interest calculation and can request a breakdown from their relationship team.

title: Val-Brume lending desk adds appointments for French-speaking businesses
author: Tomas Arlen
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank has added twelve weekly appointments at its Val-Brume lending desk for businesses that prefer to discuss borrowing in French. The additional sessions are available on Tuesdays and Thursdays and can be held at the branch or by telephone.

Appointments cover working capital, equipment purchases and reviews of existing facilities. Businesses can request a document checklist in French before their meeting. The desk will also help customers identify which financial records are needed, although it cannot prepare accounts or provide independent legal advice.

There is no appointment charge and no obligation to apply for a loan. Lending decisions remain subject to the bank’s usual affordability and security checks. The expansion follows a six-week booking review in which the Val-Brume team recorded an average wait of nine working days for a French-language lending appointment.

title: Bank publishes revised fees for business lending administration
author: Leonie Venn
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank has published a revised schedule of business lending administration fees, taking effect on 5 October. The fee for a borrower-requested security amendment will fall from KRN 450 to KRN 325. Providing a duplicate annual interest certificate will become free, replacing the current KRN 35 charge.

The fee for reviewing a request to extend an overdraft temporarily will rise from KRN 175 to KRN 225. It covers the review and does not guarantee approval. Customers will be told whether a charge applies before they ask the bank to proceed with any chargeable work.

The changes do not alter agreed loan margins or repayment dates. Where an existing agreement fixes an administration fee, that agreement will continue to apply. The full schedule is available from relationship teams and on the bank’s website, with copies in French available for customers in Val-Brume.

title: New borrower support team offers earlier repayment difficulty reviews
author: Devran Holt
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank has established a dedicated borrower support team for business customers facing repayment difficulties. The five-person team is based in Saltmarsh and accepts referrals from relationship managers across Kestria. Customers can also ask their usual lending contact for a support review.

The team will examine recent trading, cash forecasts and existing repayment commitments. Depending on the circumstances, options may include changing payment dates or agreeing a temporary reduction in principal repayments. Any arrangement requires an assessment and written agreement. Interest may continue to accrue, and extending a loan can increase its total cost.

There is no charge for the initial support review. Customers are encouraged to make contact as soon as they expect a shortfall, even if every payment is currently up to date. French-language reviews are available through the Val-Brume lending desk. Requesting a review does not itself change contractual payment obligations.

title: Half-year results show lending growth and higher impairment charges
author: Mara Ellery
body:
Harrow & Finch Bank today reported profit before tax of KRN 18.6 million for the six months ended 30 September 2026, compared with KRN 17.9 million a year earlier. Operating income rose to KRN 52.4 million from KRN 48.7 million, while operating costs increased to KRN 27.1 million from KRN 25.6 million.

The charge for expected lending losses increased to KRN 6.7 million from KRN 5.2 million. The increase mainly reflected weaker repayment prospects among a small number of wholesale borrowers. Gross customer lending reached KRN 1.24 billion at the period end, up from KRN 1.17 billion on 31 March 2026.

New lending drawn during the half year totalled KRN 186 million. Customer deposits stood at KRN 1.41 billion on 30 September. The bank continued to fund equipment purchases and working capital across Kestria while reviewing borrowers showing early signs of payment difficulty. The results are unaudited.

title: Half-year sales rise as GreenBasket reports lower operating profit
author: Daniel Rooke
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets, Kestria's largest supermarket chain by store count, reported revenue of KRN 6.42 billion for the 26 weeks ended 30 August 2026, up 4.1 per cent on the comparable period. Sales at stores open for at least a year rose 2.7 per cent.

Operating profit fell from KRN 206 million to KRN 193 million. Higher wage and refrigeration maintenance costs outweighed savings in distribution. GreenBasket invested KRN 118 million in stores, equipment and delivery vehicles during the period, including the Eastmere opening in Amberford. It ended the half year with 215 stores.

Finance director Anika Pell said customers were buying more own-label groceries and making smaller, more frequent trips. Own-label products accounted for 58 per cent of grocery units sold, compared with 55 per cent a year earlier. Online orders represented 9.4 per cent of revenue, up from 8.7 per cent in the comparable period.

title: New Val-Brume supermarket brings GreenBasket network to 216 stores
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets opened its 216th store today in the Montelier district of Val-Brume. The KRN 8.6 million investment has created 62 jobs. The store has 2,100 square metres of sales space and includes a bakery, fresh fish counter and covered collection bays for online orders.

Signs, customer information and checkout instructions are available in French, reflecting the language used across the region. Store manager Lucien Varel said all customer-facing teams included French-speaking colleagues. The opening range includes cheese, preserves and baked goods from 29 regional producers, with supplier names displayed beside the products.

The building occupies a former storage yard that had stood empty for six years. GreenBasket retained the site's boundary trees and installed a rainwater tank for cleaning outdoor areas. A pedestrian entrance connects directly with the Montelier footpath, while bicycle stands and customer parking are located on opposite sides of the building.

title: GreenBasket recalls selected oat biscuits after incorrect allergen labelling
author: Sofia Merrow
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets is recalling its 250-gram Honeyfield Oat Biscuits with batch code HB0902 and a best-before date of 18 February 2027. The affected packs contain milk, which is missing from the allergen statement. They are unsuitable for people with a milk allergy.

The biscuits were sold in 87 GreenBasket stores across Kestria between 3 and 8 September. Customers with a milk allergy should not eat them. Anyone who bought an affected pack can return it to any GreenBasket store for a full refund without a receipt. Other batch codes are not included in this recall.

GreenBasket identified the error during a packaging check yesterday and removed the affected stock from sale that evening. Recall notices are displayed in the relevant stores and on the customer website. Product safety manager Orla Venn said the company had received no reports of illness linked to the affected batch.

title: Refitted Kestrel Bay store adds quieter shopping sessions
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has completed a KRN 3.8 million refurbishment of its Harbour Steps store in Kestrel Bay. The shop remained open throughout the eight-week project. Work included replacement refrigeration, clearer aisle signs and a redesigned entrance with more space around baskets and trolleys.

The store now offers quieter shopping sessions on Tuesday and Thursday mornings between nine and ten. During these sessions, background music is switched off, routine announcements are suspended and colleagues reduce trolley movements on the shop floor. Essential safety announcements remain in use.

Customer services lead Elian Dacre said the changes followed comments from 164 shoppers who took part in a local survey. The refurbishment also added a seated service point for customers who find standing difficult. Printed store maps are available at the entrance, and colleagues can provide help finding products throughout opening hours.

title: Small suppliers receive shorter payment terms under new purchasing policy
author: Idris Weller
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has introduced payment terms of 14 calendar days for qualifying small suppliers, replacing its previous standard of 30 days. The policy applies to new purchase orders issued from today. A total of 186 existing suppliers meet the published eligibility rules.

Suppliers qualify if their annual turnover is below KRN 12 million and they employ fewer than 50 people. Payment is measured from receipt of a valid invoice after delivery. GreenBasket has removed the administration charge previously applied when suppliers requested payment before their contractual due date.

Procurement director Nella Corven said smaller producers often paid wages and bought materials well before receiving money for their goods. A dedicated accounts team in Saltmarsh now handles questions about the scheme. Suppliers can check eligibility and invoice status through their existing account, or request the same information by telephone.

title: GreenBasket opens new neighbourhood store in eastern Amberford
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets opened its Eastmere store in Amberford today, bringing its network to 215 shops across Kestria. The 1,420-square-metre store employs 46 people, including 31 colleagues recruited locally. It has eight staffed checkouts, a bakery and a collection desk for online orders.

The store stocks bread, dairy products and vegetables from 23 suppliers based within 80 kilometres of Amberford. Shelf labels identify where these products come from. Customers can buy loose portions of 34 fruit and vegetable lines, with weighing scales beside the produce section.

Store manager Tessa Brindle said the layout had been tested with residents before opening. Changes included wider gaps between promotional displays and lower shelving near the entrance. The store also has step-free access, two accessible checkout lanes and a covered seating area beside the main doors.

title: Ostara depot changes cut damaged produce deliveries by nearly a quarter
author: Idris Weller
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has reduced damaged fruit and vegetable deliveries from its Ostara depot by 24 per cent following changes to packing and loading. The result compares damage recorded per thousand crates during July to September with the same three months of 2025.

The depot supplies 68 stores and handles about 410,000 produce crates each month. Changes included shallower crates for soft fruit, separate loading positions for heavier root vegetables and temperature checks at each loading bay. GreenBasket spent KRN 1.7 million on equipment and training for the work.

Depot manager Brenna Holt said staff had recorded where damage occurred before changing handling routines. The measured reduction represents approximately 7,800 fewer damaged crates over the quarter. Produce rejected by stores remains subject to the same quality checks, and items suitable for sale are assessed separately from stock that must be discarded.

title: GreenBasket publishes clearer rules for supplier deductions and invoice disputes
author: Idris Weller
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has introduced a supplier code covering invoice disputes, delivery deductions and changes to orders. Effective today, the code requires buyers to provide written reasons and supporting records before making a deduction. It applies to all goods suppliers across the company's 216 stores.

Suppliers now have a single route for challenging deductions through a commercial review team separate from their usual buyer. The code sets a ten-working-day deadline for an initial written response. Undisputed invoice amounts remain payable under the supplier's agreed terms while a challenge is examined.

Procurement director Nella Corven said discussions with 73 suppliers had highlighted inconsistent explanations for shortages and damaged deliveries. The new code also requires written agreement before suppliers are charged for a promotion. It does not change the 14-day payment terms for eligible small businesses, whose first payment report was published yesterday.

title: First payment report shows progress for GreenBasket small suppliers
author: Daniel Rooke
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has published its first payment report since introducing 14-day terms for qualifying small suppliers on 26 August. Of the 2,460 invoices due under the scheme by 30 September, 96.2 per cent were paid within the agreed period. Average payment time was 12.6 calendar days.

The report covers invoices with a combined value of KRN 18.4 million. Ninety-four were paid late, most following internal approval delays. All 94 had been settled by 9 October. GreenBasket has added a daily review of approaching payment deadlines and assigned a named contact to each participating supplier.

Finance director Anika Pell said the late payments fell short of the company's commitment. The report lists disputed invoices separately and does not count them as paid on time. Seventeen invoices remained in dispute at the reporting date, with reasons supplied to the businesses concerned. The figures cover the small-supplier scheme rather than GreenBasket's entire supplier base.
