title: Small suppliers receive shorter payment terms under new purchasing policy
author: Idris Weller
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has introduced payment terms of 14 calendar days for qualifying small suppliers, replacing its previous standard of 30 days. The policy applies to new purchase orders issued from today. A total of 186 existing suppliers meet the published eligibility rules.

Suppliers qualify if their annual turnover is below KRN 12 million and they employ fewer than 50 people. Payment is measured from receipt of a valid invoice after delivery. GreenBasket has removed the administration charge previously applied when suppliers requested payment before their contractual due date.

Procurement director Nella Corven said smaller producers often paid wages and bought materials well before receiving money for their goods. A dedicated accounts team in Saltmarsh now handles questions about the scheme. Suppliers can check eligibility and invoice status through their existing account, or request the same information by telephone.

title: GreenBasket lowers prices on  eighty everyday grocery products nationwide
author: Sofia Merrow
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has reduced regular shelf prices on 80 everyday grocery products across all 216 stores and its online shop. The changes took effect today and cover selected bread, rice, pasta, milk and household cleaning products. No membership or minimum purchase is required.

A one-kilogram bag of GreenBasket long-grain rice now costs KRN 14.20, down from KRN 15.80. A 500-gram pack of dried pasta has fallen from KRN 9.40 to KRN 8.60. Across the 80 products, the average price reduction is 6.3 per cent, calculated without weighting for sales volumes.

Commercial director Rowan Selwick said the reductions were funded through lower packaging costs, simpler product ranges and reduced handling expenses. Existing supplier payment terms remain in force. Stores display the previous and current prices beside affected products, and the full list is available at customer service desks and on the GreenBasket website.

title: GreenBasket publishes clearer rules for supplier deductions and invoice disputes
author: Idris Weller
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has introduced a supplier code covering invoice disputes, delivery deductions and changes to orders. Effective today, the code requires buyers to provide written reasons and supporting records before making a deduction. It applies to all goods suppliers across the company's 216 stores.

Suppliers now have a single route for challenging deductions through a commercial review team separate from their usual buyer. The code sets a ten-working-day deadline for an initial written response. Undisputed invoice amounts remain payable under the supplier's agreed terms while a challenge is examined.

Procurement director Nella Corven said discussions with 73 suppliers had highlighted inconsistent explanations for shortages and damaged deliveries. The new code also requires written agreement before suppliers are charged for a promotion. It does not change the 14-day payment terms for eligible small businesses, whose first payment report was published yesterday.

title: First payment report shows progress for GreenBasket small suppliers
author: Daniel Rooke
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has published its first payment report since introducing 14-day terms for qualifying small suppliers on 26 August. Of the 2,460 invoices due under the scheme by 30 September, 96.2 per cent were paid within the agreed period. Average payment time was 12.6 calendar days.

The report covers invoices with a combined value of KRN 18.4 million. Ninety-four were paid late, most following internal approval delays. All 94 had been settled by 9 October. GreenBasket has added a daily review of approaching payment deadlines and assigned a named contact to each participating supplier.

Finance director Anika Pell said the late payments fell short of the company's commitment. The report lists disputed invoices separately and does not count them as paid on time. Seventeen invoices remained in dispute at the reporting date, with reasons supplied to the businesses concerned. The figures cover the small-supplier scheme rather than GreenBasket's entire supplier base.

title: Ostara depot changes cut damaged produce deliveries by nearly a quarter
author: Idris Weller
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has reduced damaged fruit and vegetable deliveries from its Ostara depot by 24 per cent following changes to packing and loading. The result compares damage recorded per thousand crates during July to September with the same three months of 2025.

The depot supplies 68 stores and handles about 410,000 produce crates each month. Changes included shallower crates for soft fruit, separate loading positions for heavier root vegetables and temperature checks at each loading bay. GreenBasket spent KRN 1.7 million on equipment and training for the work.

Depot manager Brenna Holt said staff had recorded where damage occurred before changing handling routines. The measured reduction represents approximately 7,800 fewer damaged crates over the quarter. Produce rejected by stores remains subject to the same quality checks, and items suitable for sale are assessed separately from stock that must be discarded.

title: Half-year sales rise as GreenBasket reports lower operating profit
author: Daniel Rooke
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets, Kestria's largest supermarket chain by store count, reported revenue of KRN 6.42 billion for the 26 weeks ended 30 August 2026, up 4.1 per cent on the comparable period. Sales at stores open for at least a year rose 2.7 per cent.

Operating profit fell from KRN 206 million to KRN 193 million. Higher wage and refrigeration maintenance costs outweighed savings in distribution. GreenBasket invested KRN 118 million in stores, equipment and delivery vehicles during the period, including the Eastmere opening in Amberford. It ended the half year with 215 stores.

Finance director Anika Pell said customers were buying more own-label groceries and making smaller, more frequent trips. Own-label products accounted for 58 per cent of grocery units sold, compared with 55 per cent a year earlier. Online orders represented 9.4 per cent of revenue, up from 8.7 per cent in the comparable period.

title: New Val-Brume supermarket brings GreenBasket network to 216 stores
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets opened its 216th store today in the Montelier district of Val-Brume. The KRN 8.6 million investment has created 62 jobs. The store has 2,100 square metres of sales space and includes a bakery, fresh fish counter and covered collection bays for online orders.

Signs, customer information and checkout instructions are available in French, reflecting the language used across the region. Store manager Lucien Varel said all customer-facing teams included French-speaking colleagues. The opening range includes cheese, preserves and baked goods from 29 regional producers, with supplier names displayed beside the products.

The building occupies a former storage yard that had stood empty for six years. GreenBasket retained the site's boundary trees and installed a rainwater tank for cleaning outdoor areas. A pedestrian entrance connects directly with the Montelier footpath, while bicycle stands and customer parking are located on opposite sides of the building.

title: GreenBasket recalls selected oat biscuits after incorrect allergen labelling
author: Sofia Merrow
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets is recalling its 250-gram Honeyfield Oat Biscuits with batch code HB0902 and a best-before date of 18 February 2027. The affected packs contain milk, which is missing from the allergen statement. They are unsuitable for people with a milk allergy.

The biscuits were sold in 87 GreenBasket stores across Kestria between 3 and 8 September. Customers with a milk allergy should not eat them. Anyone who bought an affected pack can return it to any GreenBasket store for a full refund without a receipt. Other batch codes are not included in this recall.

GreenBasket identified the error during a packaging check yesterday and removed the affected stock from sale that evening. Recall notices are displayed in the relevant stores and on the customer website. Product safety manager Orla Venn said the company had received no reports of illness linked to the affected batch.

title: Refitted Kestrel Bay store adds quieter shopping sessions
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
GreenBasket Supermarkets has completed a KRN 3.8 million refurbishment of its Harbour Steps store in Kestrel Bay. The shop remained open throughout the eight-week project. Work included replacement refrigeration, clearer aisle signs and a redesigned entrance with more space around baskets and trolleys.

The store now offers quieter shopping sessions on Tuesday and Thursday mornings between nine and ten. During these sessions, background music is switched off, routine announcements are suspended and colleagues reduce trolley movements on the shop floor. Essential safety announcements remain in use.

Customer services lead Elian Dacre said the changes followed comments from 164 shoppers who took part in a local survey. The refurbishment also added a seated service point for customers who find standing difficult. Printed store maps are available at the entrance, and colleagues can provide help finding products throughout opening hours.

title: Kestrel Bay branch sets temporary hours during roof repairs
author: Tobin Rusk
body:
Lumen Home Retail will shorten opening hours at its Kestrel Bay Harbour Lane branch while contractors replace part of the roof. From 5 to 16 October, the store will open from 9 am to 6 pm each day. Its usual opening hours are 7 am to 9 pm.

A routine building inspection found worn seals above the homeware stockroom. The affected storage area has been cleared, and work will take place behind a separate barrier. The repair budget is KRN 640,000. Grocery shopping, the pharmacy counter and customer toilets will remain available during the temporary opening hours.

Online collection customers with bookings outside the revised hours will be contacted directly and offered another slot or free home delivery. Staff will retain their contracted pay, with some shifts moved to stock preparation and nearby delivery operations. Lumen expects normal hours to resume on 17 October, subject to the final building inspection.

title: Vegetable growers join longer supply programme for Kestrian produce
author: Mara Selwick
body:
Lumen Home Retail has agreed a two-year vegetable supply programme with Reedplain Growers, a group of 18 farms outside Amberford. The programme covers potatoes, carrots, onions and cabbages sold in Lumen stores across Kestria. The first deliveries under the new terms begin on 1 October.

The agreement sets minimum purchase volumes for each crop and provides a quarterly review of growing, packing and transport costs. Lumen expects to buy about 6,400 tonnes during the first year. Orders will include smaller and unevenly shaped vegetables for its lower-priced cooking bags, provided they meet the same freshness requirements as other produce.

Participating farms will receive payment within 14 days of an accepted delivery. Lumen will share a rolling 12-week forecast, updated each week, to help growers plan harvesting and labour. Produce labels will identify the growing area, while store teams will receive guidance on storage temperatures and handling to reduce damage between delivery and sale.

title: Lumen agrees new credit facility to support planned store investment
author: Daren Pell
body:
Lumen Home Retail has signed a KRN 120 million revolving credit facility with Brackenmere Commercial Bank and Ternfold Lending. The facility matures in September 2030 and replaces a KRN 90 million agreement that was due to expire next year. It provides funds that Lumen can draw and repay as needed.

At signing, KRN 28 million was drawn under the new agreement to repay the outstanding balance on the previous facility. The remaining capacity is available for seasonal stock purchases and planned investment in stores and distribution equipment. No shares were issued as part of the financing.

Finance director Sella Morven said the agreement gave Lumen greater certainty over funding while retaining room for quieter trading periods. Interest is charged at a variable reference rate plus an agreed margin. The facility includes quarterly borrowing and interest-cover tests. Lumen met those requirements at signing and has not changed its full-year investment budget of KRN 34 million.

title: New Ostara bakery agreement brings daily deliveries to more stores
author: Mara Selwick
body:
Lumen Home Retail has signed a three-year supply agreement with Hearthmere Baking, a family-owned producer based in Ostara. From 21 September, the bakery will supply bread and rolls to 14 Lumen stores, extending an existing arrangement covering six branches. The agreement is worth an estimated KRN 7.2 million over its term.

Hearthmere has installed an additional oven and created nine production and packing jobs to support the wider service. Deliveries will reach stores before opening on six mornings each week. The range includes a small sliced loaf developed after customers asked for more choices suited to smaller households.

Lumen will provide weekly order forecasts and pay agreed invoices within 21 days. Both businesses will review unsold quantities each month, with the aim of reducing surplus without leaving shelves empty late in the day. Existing bakery suppliers will continue serving Lumen stores outside the expanded delivery area.

title: Amberford store introduces earlier collections and a simpler entrance
author: Tobin Rusk
body:
Lumen Home Retail has completed a KRN 1.8 million refurbishment of its Amberford Millgate store. The work adds a separate collection counter beside the main entrance, wider aisles in the grocery section and clearer signs for household essentials. The store remained open throughout the six-week project.

Customers can now collect online orders from 7 am, one hour earlier than before. The counter has space for chilled orders and eight numbered collection bays outside. Lumen has added 12 roles at the store, taking its workforce to 96, with recruitment completed locally.

Store manager Orla Fenwick said feedback from customers had shaped the entrance layout, particularly the position of baskets and the service desk. The refurbishment also includes enclosed refrigerated cabinets and new lighting. Lumen will compare electricity use over the next three months with the same period last year before deciding whether to extend those changes to other stores.

title: Lumen reports steady sales growth across food and home ranges
author: Elira Venn
body:
Lumen Home Retail recorded sales of KRN 486 million in the 13 weeks ended 29 August, an increase of 4.1% on the same period last year. Sales at stores open for at least a year rose by 2.3%. Grocery sales grew most strongly, while demand for kitchen storage and everyday bedding also improved.

The retailer ended the period with 42 stores across Kestria. Online orders accounted for 8.6% of sales, compared with 7.9% a year earlier. Collection orders increased particularly quickly in Saltmarsh and Amberford, where additional collection slots were introduced during the quarter.

Chief executive Neris Talven said customers remained careful about larger purchases and were comparing prices closely. Lumen kept prices unchanged on its 150-item Everyday Basket throughout the quarter. Higher delivery costs were partly offset by fuller vehicle loads and lower food waste. The company maintained its existing expectations for the financial year.

title: Val-Brume stores introduce clearer French labels across household essentials
author: Elira Venn
body:
Lumen Home Retail has introduced clearer French-language shelf labels at its three Val-Brume stores. The change covers 2,300 household and grocery products, including cleaning supplies, bedding and cupboard staples. Product names, pack sizes and unit prices now appear together in a larger, consistent format.

The work follows an eight-week review with customers and store colleagues in Kestria's French-speaking region. Participants said that unit prices were sometimes difficult to locate and that several household product descriptions needed simpler wording. Printed guidance at service desks and online collection instructions have also been revised.

The project cost KRN 210,000, including translation, printing and staff training. It does not change product prices or the ranges stocked. Lumen will collect feedback at the three stores through November and check a sample of labels each week for accuracy. Customers can report unclear wording at any service desk or through the retailer's website.

title: Lumen outlines Saltmarsh depot upgrade ahead of winter trading
author: Elira Venn
body:

Installation is scheduled to begin on 2 November and finish in stages by mid-December. The project forms part of the retailer's existing KRN 34 million annual investment budget.

The upgrade will add 320 chilled pallet spaces and replace two ageing conveyor sections used for household goods. Lumen expects the changes to reduce manual handling and give stores more flexibility when ordering fresh food. The depot currently supplies 27 of the company's 42 stores, including branches in Ostara and Val-Brume.

Work will take place in separate sections while normal deliveries continue. Lumen has leased temporary chilled storage for the installation period and scheduled staff training before each new section enters use. Eight maintenance and warehouse roles are being recruited. The company expects to assess delivery accuracy and equipment reliability after the upgraded sections have operated for eight weeks.

title: Kestrel Bay store resumes full hours after completed roof repairs
author: Tobin Rusk
body:
Lumen Home Retail's Harbour Lane store in Kestrel Bay resumed its usual 7 am to 9 pm opening hours on 17 October, following completion of roof repairs. The final inspection was completed on 16 October, allowing the homeware stockroom to return to use before the store reopened the following morning.

The work replaced worn roof seals and a damaged section of insulation above the stockroom. The final cost was KRN 618,000, compared with the KRN 640,000 budget. Contractors completed the repairs within the planned period, and the grocery section remained open throughout the temporary reduction in hours.

During the work, 286 collection bookings were moved to alternative times and 74 customers accepted free home delivery. Store manager Iven Rosk thanked customers for adjusting their visits and staff for covering revised shifts. The temporary collection arrangements have now ended, and the full homeware range is available on the shop floor again.

The agreement sets minimum purchase volumes for each crop and provides a quarterly review of growing, packing and transport costs. Lumen expects to buy about 6,400 tonnes during the first year. Orders will include smaller and unevenly shaped vegetables for its lower-priced cooking bags, provided they meet the same freshness requirements as other produce.

Participating farms will receive payment within 14 days of an accepted delivery. Lumen will share a rolling 12-week forecast, updated each week, to help growers plan harvesting and labour. Produce labels will identify the growing area, while store teams will receive guidance on storage temperatures and handling to reduce damage between delivery and sale.

title: Lumen agrees new credit facility to support planned store investment
author: Daren Pell
body:
Lumen Home Retail has signed a KRN 120 million revolving credit facility with Brackenmere Commercial Bank and Ternfold Lending. The facility matures in September 2030 and replaces a KRN 90 million agreement that was due to expire next year. It provides funds that Lumen can draw and repay as needed.

At signing, KRN 28 million was drawn under the new agreement to repay the outstanding balance on the previous facility. The remaining capacity is available for seasonal stock purchases and planned investment in stores and distribution equipment. No shares were issued as part of the financing.

Finance director Sella Morven said the agreement gave Lumen greater certainty over funding while retaining room for quieter trading periods. Interest is charged at a variable reference rate plus an agreed margin. The facility includes quarterly borrowing and interest-cover tests. Lumen met those requirements at signing and has not changed its full-year investment budget of KRN 34 million.

title: New Ostara bakery agreement brings daily deliveries to more stores
author: Mara Selwick
body:
Lumen Home Retail has signed a three-year supply agreement with Hearthmere Baking, a family-owned producer based in Ostara. From 21 September, the bakery will supply bread and rolls to 14 Lumen stores, extending an existing arrangement covering six branches. The agreement is worth an estimated KRN 7.2 million over its term.

Hearthmere has installed an additional oven and created nine production and packing jobs to support the wider service. Deliveries will reach stores before opening on six mornings each week. The range includes a small sliced loaf developed after customers asked for more choices suited to smaller households.

Lumen will provide weekly order forecasts and pay agreed invoices within 21 days. Both businesses will review unsold quantities each month, with the aim of reducing surplus without leaving shelves empty late in the day. Existing bakery suppliers will continue serving Lumen stores outside the expanded delivery area.

title: Corvel updates carton prices following higher board costs
author: Ellis Dacre
body:
Corvel Packaging has increased base prices for newly quoted folding cartons by an average of 3.4 per cent from today. Individual changes range from 2.1 to 4.6 per cent, depending on board grade, carton weight and print requirements. Confirmed orders retain their agreed base prices.

The adjustment follows higher delivered board costs recorded during August and September. It applies to cartons produced at Amberford and does not change the base prices of trays or films. The energy surcharge remains separate at KRN 58 per tonne and is calculated using dispatch weight.

Revised quotations show the base price and estimated surcharge separately so customers can compare the full cost at a stated order quantity. Existing written quotations remain valid until their stated expiry dates. Account teams can review board grades or order sizes with customers, although any specification change still requires approval before production.

title: Ostara tray plant cuts trim waste through tooling changes
author: Tobin Merrow
body:
Corvel Packaging's Ostara plant has reduced trim waste on two chilled-food tray lines following changes to cutting tools and sheet positioning. Across eight weeks of measured production, trim represented 13.1 per cent of material fed into the lines, down from 16.4 per cent during the preceding eight weeks.

The comparison covers the same four tray designs and excludes trial runs. Staff adjusted the spacing between tray shapes and replaced worn cutting edges. The plant used 18 tonnes less sheet material than it would have used at the earlier trim rate for the recorded volume.

Tray dimensions, sealing surfaces and approved material specifications are unchanged. Clean trim from these lines is separated for controlled reprocessing, subject to the requirements of each product specification. Corvel is reporting the reduction as a material efficiency measure; it has not calculated a carbon saving from the work.

title: Energy surcharge rises as packaging production costs increase
author: Ellis Dacre
body:
Corvel Packaging has increased its energy surcharge from KRN 42 to KRN 58 per tonne for goods dispatched from today. The rate covers cartons, trays and films made at its three production sites. Base prices remain unchanged under this adjustment.

Purchased energy costs have risen further since the surcharge was introduced on 31 August. The latest four weeks of production records show an average energy cost increase of KRN 67 per tonne against the company's May reference level. Corvel is absorbing the difference between that increase and the surcharge.

An order containing 2.5 tonnes of packaging now carries a surcharge of KRN 145 before tax. The dispatch date determines the applicable rate, including for orders placed earlier. Invoice weight details remain available by product line. Customers with a fixed-price agreement should refer to its surcharge terms or contact their account manager for an explanation.

title: Corvel publishes clearer weight details on packaging invoices
author: Nadia Pell
body:
Corvel Packaging has updated its invoices to show the net packaging weight used to calculate its energy surcharge. The revised layout lists product weight, surcharge rate and surcharge value together. Pallets, outer wrapping and returnable transport frames are excluded from the calculation.

The change follows questions received when the KRN 42 per tonne surcharge took effect yesterday. For mixed deliveries, each product line carries its own weight and charge. Where an order is split between dispatches, the invoice includes only the quantity sent in that delivery.

Customers can also obtain the same weight breakdown from their account contact without requesting a replacement invoice. Corvel has checked the revised layout against 30 sample orders covering cartons, trays and films. The checks found no change to the amount charged; the update makes the calculation easier to follow and compare with delivery records.

title: Corvel introduces separate energy surcharge on food packaging orders
author: Ellis Dacre
body:
Corvel Packaging has introduced an energy surcharge of KRN 42 per tonne on cartons, trays and films dispatched from today. The charge applies to domestic orders across Kestria and appears as a separate invoice line. Base product prices are unchanged.

The surcharge reflects higher electricity and process heating costs at the company's Amberford, Ostara and Kestrel Bay plants. Corvel's combined energy cost per tonne of finished packaging was 14 per cent higher in August than in May, despite lower consumption on several production lines.

For an order weighing 2.5 tonnes, the surcharge is KRN 105 before tax. It does not apply to goods dispatched before today, even where the invoice is issued later. Customer statements show the dispatch weight used in the calculation, and account teams have received a common worksheet to explain the charge and resolve weight queries.

title: Corvel Packaging adds carton capacity at Amberford plant
author: Mara Venn
body:
Corvel Packaging has brought a second carton folding line into service at its Amberford plant. The line adds capacity for 1.8 million food cartons a month, increasing the site's monthly folding capacity to 7.2 million units. It handles sleeves and folding cartons used for chilled meals, bakery products and dry foods.

Installation and production trials cost KRN 4.6 million. During acceptance checks, staff ran six carton sizes and measured fold accuracy, glue application and print alignment. Twelve employees have completed training on the equipment, including operators transferred from the site's older finishing area.

The additional capacity addresses demand from customers in Amberford and Saltmarsh. Orders remain subject to the usual checks on board availability and artwork approval. Customers with approved carton designs can ask their account contact to review order quantities against the expanded production schedule.

title: Corvel publishes evidence sheets for selected carton recycling claims
author: Tobin Merrow
body:
Corvel Packaging has issued evidence sheets for 18 uncoated carton specifications supplied from Amberford. Each sheet identifies the board grade, coatings, inks and adhesives covered by the assessment. It also explains the conditions attached to the company's recycling statements.

The sheets draw on fibre separation tests and checks of collection guidance available in Saltmarsh, Amberford and Val-Brume. Results apply only to the listed specifications. Cartons with film windows, barrier layers or heavy food contamination require separate consideration and are outside the scope of this release.

Customers can request a sheet using their carton specification number. The documents support packaging decisions but do not establish that every local collection service accepts a carton. Corvel advises customers to check disposal wording against the collection arrangements serving their buyers. No new recycling claim has been added to customer artwork as part of this work.

title: Kestrel Bay film line returns after planned maintenance
author: Mara Venn
body:
Corvel Packaging has returned its second film line at Kestrel Bay to normal production following a four-day maintenance shutdown. Work included replacing heater controls, checking winding equipment and servicing the cooling system. The line produces sealing films for prepared-food trays.

Operators completed restart checks on three film thicknesses before releasing production. Tests covered thickness variation, roll tension and seal performance against approved tray samples. All three trial batches met their existing specifications. The work has not changed the materials used or the approved uses of the films.

Corvel supplied scheduled orders from stock built before the shutdown, and no confirmed delivery dates were missed. Both film lines at Kestrel Bay are now operating. Customers receiving material from the restarted line can find the production batch reference on each roll label and on the accompanying quality record.

title: Corvel opens French language customer desk in Val-Brume
author: Nadia Pell
body:
Corvel Packaging has opened a French language customer desk in Val-Brume to support food producers in Kestria's French-speaking region. Three customer service staff now handle order enquiries, delivery updates and invoice questions from the office. The desk operates on weekdays from 08:30 to 17:00 local time.

Customers can request quotations, specification summaries and surcharge explanations in French. Technical approval remains with the production site responsible for the packaging. The desk uses the same order records as Corvel's Saltmarsh team, allowing staff to check quantities and dispatch information without creating a separate customer account.

The office supports customers buying cartons, trays and films; it does not hold stock or receive returned goods. During its internal service trial, staff handled 64 sample enquiries covering all three product groups. Customers already assigned an account manager retain that contact and can use the new desk for routine order support.

title: Corvel adds recycled content option for selected food trays
author: Tobin Merrow
body:
Corvel Packaging has added a tray material containing 35 per cent recycled plastic by weight to its Ostara product range. The option is available for two clear chilled-food tray sizes. It uses recycled material from a controlled process assessed for the specified food contact conditions.

Qualification checks covered material traceability, tray strength, sealing and migration under chilled storage conditions. The trays are approved for the listed chilled foods and temperatures in their technical sheets. They are not approved for oven use. Customers must confirm that their intended food and filling process match those conditions.

The recycled content figure applies to the tray body and excludes any lid, label or absorbent pad. Batch records identify the material blend used in production. Initial supply is available in minimum orders of 40,000 trays per size, with pricing provided by quotation. Existing tray specifications remain available for customers with different requirements.

title: Amberford carton line completes first full production month
author: Mara Venn
body:
Corvel Packaging's new Amberford folding line produced 1.42 million saleable cartons during September, its first full calendar month in service. The line entered production on 25 August and has a rated monthly capacity of 1.8 million cartons under the company's standard shift pattern.

September output covered 23 customer designs, including chilled-meal sleeves and bakery cartons. Average time between completing one job and starting the next fell from 74 minutes in the first production week to 56 minutes in the final week. Operators recorded these times using the same changeover checklist.

The plant dispatched 96 per cent of September carton orders on their confirmed dates, compared with 92 per cent in August. Corvel attributes the improvement partly to the additional line and partly to steadier board deliveries. The figures cover all Amberford carton orders, rather than only work assigned to the new equipment.

title: Corvel expands returnable pallet scheme after Saltmarsh customer trial
author: Nadia Pell
body:
Corvel Packaging has expanded its returnable pallet scheme to regular delivery routes serving Amberford and Val-Brume. The scheme follows a 12-week trial with eight food producers in Saltmarsh. Participating customers returned 438 of the 480 pallets issued during the trial.

Of the returned pallets, 421 passed inspection for reuse and 17 required repair. Corvel records each pallet by reference number and collects empty pallets during an agreed delivery visit. The scheme uses a refundable deposit of KRN 85 per pallet, shown separately from packaging and transport charges.

Customers need a dry storage area and enough space to hold pallets safely between collections. Deposits are credited after return and inspection, subject to the scheme's damage terms. Availability depends on the delivery route and collection space. The trial measured returns and condition; Corvel has not used those results to publish a carbon saving claim.

title: Corvel lowers energy surcharge following reduced purchased power costs
author: Ellis Dacre
body:
Corvel Packaging has reduced its energy surcharge from KRN 58 to KRN 31 per tonne for goods dispatched from today. The lower rate applies to cartons, trays and films across its production sites. It replaces the rate introduced on 22 September.

The reduction follows lower purchased electricity costs and reduced heating demand during the latest four-week review period. Energy costs remain above the May reference level used when Corvel introduced the surcharge. The company continues to calculate the charge separately from product base prices.

For a delivery weighing 2.5 tonnes, the surcharge is now KRN 77.50 before tax, a reduction of KRN 67.50. Goods dispatched before today retain the rate applicable on their dispatch date. The carton base price adjustment introduced on 30 September remains in place because it reflects board costs. Customers can obtain a breakdown of both elements from their account contact.

title: Harvest Review Trims Wheat Estimate As Oat Outlook Holds
body:
AMBERFORD, Kestria, Sept. 28, 2026 /KestriaWire/ -- Prairie Gold Grain Co-operative has revised its member wheat harvest estimate to 179,500 tonnes, down from the August estimate of 184,000 tonnes. The oat estimate is now 52,400 tonnes, compared with 52,000 tonnes previously. The review uses completed field records and updated reports received by 27 September.

Lower wheat yields around Ostara account for most of the reduction. Amberford results remain close to the earlier estimate. Members report that 81 per cent of their wheat area and 69 per cent of their oat area has been harvested, leaving uncertainty around the remaining fields.

The co-operative has accepted 96,800 tonnes of wheat and 21,600 tonnes of oats into its stores. These intake figures exclude grain still held on farms and must not be added to the harvest estimate. Customer allocations remain covered by accepted stocks and grain secured under existing member delivery agreements.

title: Rain Raises Drying Demand At Ostara Grain Receiving Site
body:
AMBERFORD, Kestria, Sept. 16, 2026 /KestriaWire/ -- Rain around Ostara has increased the proportion of wheat deliveries requiring drying at Prairie Gold Grain Co-operative's local receiving site. Of the 61 wheat loads sampled during the past two days, 24 exceeded the standard moisture limit of 14 per cent. Accepted wet grain is being stored separately.

The site's dryer has processed 460 tonnes since the rain began. Members are being given a moisture reading and an estimated drying charge before unloading. The charge depends on the moisture removed and is separate from the purchase price shown on the member's grain agreement.

Receiving staff have reduced the number of wet-grain bookings to match drying capacity. Dry wheat and oat bookings remain available, subject to storage space. Members should report their latest moisture reading when arranging a delivery and should not mix damp grain with a dry load to meet the acceptance limit.

title: September Purchase Notice Sets Wheat And Oat Base Prices
body:
KESTREL BAY, Kestria, Sept. 14, 2026 /KestriaWire/ -- Prairie Gold Grain Co-operative has set its posted purchase price at KRN 286 per tonne for standard milling wheat and KRN 218 per tonne for standard food oats. The prices apply to new purchase agreements accepted from 14 September for grain delivered to the Amberford receiving site.

The wheat price assumes moisture no higher than 14 per cent and protein of at least 12 per cent. The oat price assumes moisture no higher than 13.5 per cent and test weight of at least 52 kilogrammes per hectolitre. Other quality requirements remain available from the buying desk.

These are prices paid to supplying members, rather than delivered selling prices for customers. Haulage, drying and any agreed quality adjustments are shown separately on settlement statements. Existing fixed-price agreements retain their agreed terms. Members should obtain a purchase reference before sending grain against the new notice.

title: Early Wheat Samples Show Firm Protein And Low Moisture
body:
OSTARA, Kestria, Sept. 7, 2026 /KestriaWire/ -- The first new-season quality report from Prairie Gold Grain Co-operative shows average wheat protein of 12.6 per cent and average moisture of 13.2 per cent. The report covers 186 accepted loads, representing 5,920 tonnes delivered to the Amberford and Ostara receiving sites by 6 September.

Average wheat test weight was 78.4 kilogrammes per hectolitre. These results support the sale of several parcels for milling, although each customer contract has its own requirements. The samples mainly represent earlier-harvested fields and should not be treated as a measure of the whole crop.

Oat deliveries remain limited, with 740 tonnes accepted so far. Members can request the test results for their own loads through the receiving office. Any request for a second test must identify the delivery ticket, allowing staff to locate the sealed sample retained from that load.

title: Amberford Receiving Yard Introduces Separate Queues For Wheat And Oats
body:
KESTREL BAY, Kestria, Aug. 21, 2026 /KestriaWire/ -- Prairie Gold Grain Co-operative has introduced separate wheat and oat queues at its Amberford receiving yard. The change follows a trial involving 38 deliveries, during which the average time from arrival to unloading fell from 54 minutes to 37 minutes. Both lanes use the existing weighbridge.

body:

Measured stocks at the close of 21 October totalled 121,460 tonnes of wheat and 34,280 tonnes of oats. The figures include grain already allocated to customers but awaiting collection.

Staff compared bin measurements with receiving tickets, dispatch weights and recorded cleaning losses. The combined difference between measured grain and stock records was 0.08 per cent, within the co-operative's internal tolerance of 0.20 per cent. All four sites completed checks, and no unexplained difference required a customer allocation to be changed.

Routine temperature readings also found no storage parcel above the co-operative's action threshold of 20 degrees. Store teams continue to check grain condition and record aeration work. Customers requesting available volumes should contact the sales desk, as total physical stock includes committed grain and parcels held for further preparation.

Members supplied harvested area and weighed production records, with separate estimates for the small amount of grain retained in unweighed farm bins.

Co-operative stores have received 158,600 tonnes of wheat and 44,800 tonnes of oats from this harvest. The balance remains on farms for later delivery, farm use or other sales. title: Bramble Foods pays interim dividend of twelve crowns cents
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
Bramble Foods today paid its interim dividend of KRN 0.12 per ordinary share to shareholders who were on the register on 4 September 2026. The payment follows the dividend declaration included in the company's half-year results on 17 August. The total distribution is KRN 7.2 million.

Shareholders receiving payment by bank transfer should allow for their bank's normal processing times. Those who have elected to receive paper payment notices will receive them at their registered address. Dividend statements are also available through the company's shareholder account service.

Investors who have recently changed their address or bank details should check that their shareholder records are current. Bramble Foods' investor relations team in Saltmarsh can explain how to submit updates securely. The company will issue its next scheduled trading update on 19 October, covering revenue and trading conditions for the three months ended 30 September.

title: New oat cracker range reaches Kestrian shops this month
author: Tobin Vale
body:
Bramble Foods will begin supplying its new Bramble Table oat crackers to retailers on 28 September. The range comprises plain oat, toasted onion and garden herb varieties in 180 gram packs. Distribution will start in Saltmarsh and Ostara before extending to other parts of Kestria during October.

The crackers are made at the company's Ostara snacks plant using an existing baking line adapted during the summer. Bramble Foods has invested KRN 620,000 in mixing equipment and product development. The recommended retail price is KRN 2.80 per pack, although individual retailers will set their own selling prices.

Development included tasting sessions with 240 adult volunteers and checks on breakage during transport. The company has arranged an initial eight-week production programme, with later output dependent on repeat orders. Ingredient and allergen information will appear on every pack, alongside storage guidance intended to help customers keep opened crackers fresh.

title: Bramble Foods agrees purchase of Val-Brume specialist bakery
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
Bramble Foods has agreed to acquire Hearthmere Bakery, a privately owned producer of crispbreads and seeded biscuits based in Val-Brume, for KRN 24.6 million in cash. The purchase remains subject to competition clearance and customary completion conditions. Completion is expected by the end of October.

Hearthmere Bakery employs 86 people at a single production site in Kestria's French-speaking region. It recorded revenue of KRN 31.8 million in its last financial year. Its range would add specialist baked snacks to Bramble Foods' existing bakery and biscuit business.

Bramble Foods intends to retain the Hearthmere name, the Val-Brume site and its workforce. The proposed acquisition would be funded from existing cash and committed borrowing facilities. Until completion, both businesses will continue to operate independently. Bramble Foods has not included any contribution from Hearthmere in its current trading expectations and will provide a further announcement when the transaction completes.

title: Amberford bakery prepares new packing line for autumn commissioning
author: Leonie Varnet
body:
Bramble Foods has completed the main installation work on a new packing line at its Amberford bakery. The KRN 8.4 million project replaces two older machines used for small cake packs and is scheduled to enter commissioning in October. Electrical checks and staff training will take place during September.

Once fully operational, the line is expected to increase the site's cake packing capacity by 18% and reduce film waste per pack by about 11%. These estimates will be checked during production trials. The bakery will continue supplying customers through its existing equipment while the new line is tested.

The project includes 14 additional permanent roles across production, maintenance and quality control. Recruitment has begun locally, with practical training provided on site. Bramble Foods said the investment supports demand for smaller packs without requiring an extension to the bakery building. Total spending remains within the approved project budget.

title: Bramble Foods announces October price changes for selected snacks
author: Tobin Vale
body:
Bramble Foods has notified retail customers of price increases averaging 2.5% across selected biscuits and savoury snacks, effective from 1 October 2026. The changes apply to wholesale list prices in Kestria. Standard sliced bread and plain bread rolls are excluded from this announcement.

The company said higher costs for edible oils, cocoa ingredients and flexible packaging had continued through the summer. Savings from purchasing and factory improvements have absorbed part of those increases. Individual product changes will vary, and retailers will decide the prices paid by shoppers.

Bramble Foods is giving customers six weeks to update ordering systems and review planned promotions. Existing promotional agreements covering September will be honoured. Customer teams based in Saltmarsh and Kestrel Bay will provide revised price lists and product details directly to retailers. Pack weights and recipes will remain unchanged as part of this price review.

title: Bramble Foods reports higher first half sales and operating profit
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
Bramble Foods, the listed Kestrian bakery and snacks company, today reported revenue of KRN 428.6 million for the six months ended 30 June 2026, up 6.4% on the same period last year. Operating profit rose to KRN 34.2 million from KRN 30.8 million. Sales volumes increased by 2.1%, with the remaining revenue growth coming from prices and changes in the mix of products sold.

Packaged bread performed steadily, while savoury crackers and small cake packs recorded stronger growth. Lower waste at the Amberford bakery helped offset higher flour and packaging costs. Net debt at the period end was KRN 76.5 million, compared with KRN 81.3 million a year earlier.

The board declared an interim dividend of KRN 0.12 per share, payable on 30 September to shareholders registered on 4 September. Bramble Foods continues to expect modest volume growth during the second half, although household spending remains uneven across Kestria.

title: Competition clearance received for proposed Hearthmere Bakery acquisition
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
Bramble Foods has received clearance from Kestria's competition authority for its proposed acquisition of Hearthmere Bakery. The KRN 24.6 million cash transaction was announced on 18 September. Clearance satisfies one of the principal conditions of the purchase agreement, with completion still subject to the remaining customary requirements.

The companies are now preparing final completion documents and arrangements for transferring ownership. Bramble Foods continues to expect the transaction to complete by the end of October. Hearthmere remains independently owned and managed until that process has concluded.

Plans announced in September to retain Hearthmere's name, Val-Brume production site and 86 employees remain in place. Initial work following completion would focus on financial reporting, purchasing procedures and customer service arrangements. Bramble Foods said there would be no immediate changes to Hearthmere's recipes or product packaging. A separate announcement will confirm completion and the date from which Hearthmere's results enter the group accounts.

title: October snack price changes take effect across customer orders
author: Tobin Vale
body:
Bramble Foods has implemented the wholesale price changes announced on 20 August. Revised prices took effect on 1 October for selected biscuits and savoury snacks, with an average increase of 2.5% across the affected range. Standard sliced bread and plain bread rolls remain outside this review.

The company's customer service teams checked the first orders under the revised lists last week. A small number of invoice queries are being resolved directly with retailers. Deliveries have continued to schedule, and no product withdrawals or changes to pack weights have accompanied the price adjustment.

Bramble Foods said the increase addresses part of the higher ingredient and packaging costs reported during the summer. Retailers continue to set their own shelf prices and promotional offers. The company will monitor order patterns over the coming weeks, recognising that a few days of trading cannot establish how shoppers will respond to any resulting shelf price changes.

title: Bramble Foods announces October price changes for selected snacks
author: Tobin Vale
body:

title: Bramble Foods reports higher first half sales and operating profit
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
Bramble Foods, the listed Kestrian bakery and snacks company, today reported revenue of KRN 428.6 million for the six months ended 30 June 2026, up 6.4% on the same period last year. Operating profit rose to KRN 34.2 million from KRN 30.8 million. Sales volumes increased by 2.1%, with the remaining revenue growth coming from prices and changes in the mix of products sold.

Packaged bread performed steadily, while savoury crackers and small cake packs recorded stronger growth. Lower waste at the Amberford bakery helped offset higher flour and packaging costs. Net debt at the period end was KRN 76.5 million, compared with KRN 81.3 million a year earlier.

The board declared an interim dividend of KRN 0.12 per share, payable on 30 September to shareholders registered on 4 September. Bramble Foods continues to expect modest volume growth during the second half, although household spending remains uneven across Kestria.

title: Amberford packing trials meet quality targets ahead of production
author: Leonie Varnet
body:
Bramble Foods has completed the initial commissioning trials for its new cake packing line at Amberford. Trial packs met the site's checks for seal strength, weight accuracy and product protection. The line is scheduled to begin regular customer production on 19 October, initially operating on one shift.

The KRN 8.4 million investment was outlined in August. All 14 additional permanent roles have now been filled, and operators have completed supervised training. Existing packing equipment will remain available during the early production period so that the bakery can maintain deliveries if adjustments are required.

Early trials indicate that the line can support the planned increase in capacity, but Bramble Foods will assess sustained output and packaging waste over a full month of production. The company expects to add a second shift as orders require. Final project spending remains within budget, including installation, training and a supply of essential spare parts.

title: Competition clearance received for proposed Hearthmere Bakery acquisition
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
Bramble Foods has received clearance from Kestria's competition authority for its proposed acquisition of Hearthmere Bakery. The KRN 24.6 million cash transaction was announced on 18 September. Clearance satisfies one of the principal conditions of the purchase agreement, with completion still subject to the remaining customary requirements.

The companies are now preparing final completion documents and arrangements for transferring ownership. Bramble Foods continues to expect the transaction to complete by the end of October. Hearthmere remains independently owned and managed until that process has concluded.

Plans announced in September to retain Hearthmere's name, Val-Brume production site and 86 employees remain in place. Initial work following completion would focus on financial reporting, purchasing procedures and customer service arrangements. Bramble Foods said there would be no immediate changes to Hearthmere's recipes or product packaging. A separate announcement will confirm completion and the date from which Hearthmere's results enter the group accounts.

title: October snack price changes take effect across customer orders
author: Tobin Vale
body:
Bramble Foods has implemented the wholesale price changes announced on 20 August. Revised prices took effect on 1 October for selected biscuits and savoury snacks, with an average increase of 2.5% across the affected range. Standard sliced bread and plain bread rolls remain outside this review.

The company's customer service teams checked the first orders under the revised lists last week. A small number of invoice queries are being resolved directly with retailers. Deliveries have continued to schedule, and no product withdrawals or changes to pack weights have accompanied the price adjustment.

Bramble Foods said the increase addresses part of the higher ingredient and packaging costs reported during the summer. Retailers continue to set their own shelf prices and promotional offers. The company will monitor order patterns over the coming weeks, recognising that a few days of trading cannot establish how shoppers will respond to any resulting shelf price changes.

title: Bramble Foods pays interim dividend of twelve crowns cents
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
Bramble Foods today paid its interim dividend of KRN 0.12 per ordinary share to shareholders who were on the register on 4 September 2026. The payment follows the dividend declaration included in the company's half-year results on 17 August. The total distribution is KRN 7.2 million.

Shareholders receiving payment by bank transfer should allow for their bank's normal processing times. Those who have elected to receive paper payment notices will receive them at their registered address. Dividend statements are also available through the company's shareholder account service.

Investors who have recently changed their address or bank details should check that their shareholder records are current. Bramble Foods' investor relations team in Saltmarsh can explain how to submit updates securely. The company will issue its next scheduled trading update on 19 October, covering revenue and trading conditions for the three months ended 30 September.

title: New oat cracker range reaches Kestrian shops this month
author: Tobin Vale
body:
Bramble Foods will begin supplying its new Bramble Table oat crackers to retailers on 28 September. The range comprises plain oat, toasted onion and garden herb varieties in 180 gram packs. Distribution will start in Saltmarsh and Ostara before extending to other parts of Kestria during October.

The crackers are made at the company's Ostara snacks plant using an existing baking line adapted during the summer. Bramble Foods has invested KRN 620,000 in mixing equipment and product development. The recommended retail price is KRN 2.80 per pack, although individual retailers will set their own selling prices.

Development included tasting sessions with 240 adult volunteers and checks on breakage during transport. The company has arranged an initial eight-week production programme, with later output dependent on repeat orders. Ingredient and allergen information will appear on every pack, alongside storage guidance intended to help customers keep opened crackers fresh.

title: Bramble Foods agrees purchase of Val-Brume specialist bakery
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
Bramble Foods has agreed to acquire Hearthmere Bakery, a privately owned producer of crispbreads and seeded biscuits based in Val-Brume, for KRN 24.6 million in cash. The purchase remains subject to competition clearance and customary completion conditions. Completion is expected by the end of October.

Hearthmere Bakery employs 86 people at a single production site in Kestria's French-speaking region. It recorded revenue of KRN 31.8 million in its last financial year. Its range would add specialist baked snacks to Bramble Foods' existing bakery and biscuit business.

Bramble Foods intends to retain the Hearthmere name, the Val-Brume site and its workforce. The proposed acquisition would be funded from existing cash and committed borrowing facilities. Until completion, both businesses will continue to operate independently. Bramble Foods has not included any contribution from Hearthmere in its current trading expectations and will provide a further announcement when the transaction completes.

body:

Hearthmere's financial results will be included in Bramble Foods' group accounts from today.

The Val-Brume business makes crispbreads and seeded biscuits and employs 86 people. Its name, production site and workforce have been retained. Customers will continue to place orders through their existing contacts, and current supply agreements remain in effect. Product recipes and packaging are unchanged at completion.

The purchase was funded through a combination of available cash and drawings under Bramble Foods' existing borrowing facilities. During the first three months of ownership, work will concentrate on reporting systems, supplier arrangements and planning for future orders. Bramble Foods expects a small contribution to group revenue for the remainder of 2026 and will provide further detail with its full-year results.

title: Kestrel Bay bakery completes oven heat recovery installation
author: Leonie Varnet
body:
Bramble Foods has brought a new heat recovery system into service at its Kestrel Bay bakery following installation during planned maintenance. The KRN 1.3 million system captures heat from oven exhausts and uses it to warm water for cleaning. It serves two bread ovens at the site.

Engineering estimates suggest the equipment could reduce the bakery's annual purchased energy use by around 6%. Actual savings will depend on production hours and seasonal demand for hot water. Bramble Foods will compare meter readings with production volumes over the next six months before reporting a measured result.

Installation took place over three scheduled maintenance weekends, with bread deliveries maintained from existing stocks and production at other group bakeries. Maintenance staff have received training on cleaning and inspection requirements. The project forms part of the company's approved factory investment programme and does not change the site's production capacity or staffing levels.

title: Third quarter sales rise as bakery demand remains steady
author: Mara Fenwick
body:
Bramble Foods recorded revenue of KRN 219.4 million for the three months ended 30 September 2026, an increase of 4.8% compared with the same quarter last year. Revenue for the first nine months reached KRN 648.0 million. Third-quarter sales volumes grew by 1.3%, supported by steady bread demand and higher cracker sales.

Trading remained strongest in Saltmarsh and Amberford, while orders from smaller shops were more variable. The new oat cracker range began shipping near the quarter end and made only a small contribution. Wholesale price changes introduced on 1 October had no effect on the reported quarter.

The board's full-year operating profit expectations remain unchanged. Regular production on Amberford's new packing line began today, with performance monitoring under way. The proposed Hearthmere Bakery acquisition has received competition clearance but has not yet completed. Its trading is therefore excluded from these figures, and completion remains expected by the end of October.

title: Oakhill Revises Wholesale Prices Following Flour Cost Increases
author: Lucien Bréval
body:
Oakhill Bakeries Group has revised its wholesale price list, increasing prices by an average of 3.2 per cent across its bread and roll range. The new list applies from today. Customers received four weeks' written notice, including a product-by-product schedule showing the changes.

The wholesale price of a standard 800g white loaf has risen from KRN 4.10 to KRN 4.23. A pack of six plain rolls has increased from KRN 3.60 to KRN 3.72. Prices for seven products, including selected sweet buns, remain unchanged.

Oakhill's contracted flour cost is 9.1 per cent higher than under its previous supply agreement. Packaging costs have also increased. Commercial manager Nerys Fennholt said savings from production and purchasing have absorbed part of the rise. Retailers set their own selling prices, and Oakhill's delivery threshold and small-order charge remain unchanged.

title: Oakhill Opens Recruitment for New Kestrel Bay Bakery
author: Rowan Pellwick
body:
Oakhill Bakeries Group has opened recruitment for 46 permanent roles at its new Kestrel Bay bakery. Vacancies cover production, engineering, hygiene, warehousing and supervision. Construction is complete, and equipment testing is under way. The site is not yet producing goods for sale.

The bakery has a designed capacity of 20 tonnes a day and contains separate areas for bread rolls and morning goods. Oakhill has invested KRN 13.6 million in the building and equipment. Applications are open to experienced bakery workers and candidates seeking their first manufacturing role.

Production roles start at KRN 17.40 an hour, with additional payments for night work. Each vacancy states its shift pattern and guaranteed hours. Staff affected by the Ostara closure proposal can request a confidential discussion about these roles without giving up their right to take part in the consultation.

title: Oakhill Introduces Clearer Delivery Charges for Small Shops
author: Lucien Bréval
body:
Oakhill Bakeries Group has introduced a single delivery charge for small shop orders across its existing delivery network in Kestria. Orders below KRN 240 now carry a KRN 12 charge. Orders at or above that value receive delivery without a separate fee.

The change replaces six local charging arrangements that had developed as delivery routes expanded. Product prices are unchanged. Customers received individual notices and examples showing how the revised charge applies to their usual orders, including mixed orders of bread, rolls and sweet bakery products.

The same threshold applies in Saltmarsh, Kestrel Bay, Ostara, Amberford and Val-Brume. Customers can combine products on one order to reach it. Commercial manager Nerys Fennholt said the simpler arrangement makes invoices easier to check and helps shopkeepers compare the cost of placing several small orders with one larger delivery.

title: Amberford Bakery Welcomes First Intake of Paid Apprentices
author: Rowan Pellwick
body:
Eight apprentices have joined Oakhill Bakeries Group at Amberford, taking the site's workforce to 154. The paid places cover baking, engineering and food quality work. The apprentices are additional to the 22 permanent roles created by the recently opened bread hall.

Each apprentice has a named workplace mentor and receives six hours of protected learning time each week. Starting pay is KRN 15.80 an hour, with increases linked to completed training stages. Oakhill supplies work clothing, safety footwear and the materials needed for practical assessments.

The first week covers food hygiene, safe movement around machinery and basic dough preparation. Apprentices do not operate equipment without supervision. Bakery manager Iona Merewick said the intake includes school leavers and people changing careers, giving the bakery a useful mix of experience alongside staff who have worked there for many years.

title: Oakhill Begins Staff Consultation on Ostara Bakery Closure
author: Elin Veymar
body:
Oakhill Bakeries Group has begun consultation with the 31 employees at its Ostara bakery over a proposal to close the site. No final decision has been made. The bakery produces sandwich rolls and plain buns in a building with limited space for modern equipment.

The site has a daily capacity of 14 tonnes, although average output over the past six months was eight tonnes. Maintenance and energy costs per tonne have risen as production has fallen. The company is examining whether work can be transferred to its other bakeries.

Employees have received written details of the proposal and can attend individual meetings during paid working time. Oakhill is considering alternatives submitted by staff, including changes to shifts and products. Managing director Tessa Oakhill said the consultation must allow employees to question the figures and put forward workable options.

title: Oakhill Opens Expanded Bread Hall at Amberford Bakery
author: Mara Denholt
body:
Oakhill Bakeries Group has opened an expanded bread hall at its Amberford bakery, increasing the site's daily production capacity from 28 to 40 tonnes. The family-owned business invested KRN 8.4 million in the extension, which includes two ovens, cooling equipment and a separate packing area.

The hall produces sliced white bread, wholemeal loaves and bread rolls for shops across central Kestria. Its first commercial batches left the bakery this morning. Staff completed equipment checks and practice runs before production began, with each batch checked for weight, crust colour and texture.

The investment has created 22 permanent jobs, bringing employment at Amberford to 146. All new starters have completed their initial training. Managing director Tessa Oakhill said the extra space gives the bakery more room to separate baking and packing work, reducing congestion during its busiest shifts.

title: Kestrel Bay Bakery Starts Production With Local Delivery Orders
author: Mara Denholt
body:
Oakhill Bakeries Group's new Kestrel Bay bakery began commercial production today, supplying plain rolls and breakfast buns to 38 local shops. Opening output is six tonnes a day against a designed daily capacity of 20 tonnes. Orders are being added in stages as production settles.

The site employs 46 people, including eight colleagues transferring from Ostara. The team completed training, trial batches and cleaning checks before today's opening. Each production run is checked for weight, appearance and packing quality before goods are released for delivery to customers.

The KRN 13.6 million bakery has loading bays that keep incoming ingredients separate from finished goods. Bakery manager Dorian Kelwick said starting with a limited range gives staff time to establish consistent routines. Customers receiving their first deliveries have a dedicated contact for reporting shortages, damaged packs or concerns about product quality.

title: Oakhill Confirms Ostara Closure Following Employee Consultation Process
author: Elin Veymar
body:
Oakhill Bakeries Group has confirmed the closure of its Ostara bakery following consultation with employees. The decision affects 31 roles. The company considered proposals for shorter production weeks, a smaller product range and additional contract baking, but none provided enough regular work to cover the site's costs.

Nineteen employees have accepted roles elsewhere in the group: 11 at Amberford and eight at Kestrel Bay. Twelve employees remain at risk of redundancy and have received individual statements setting out their payments and support. Transfer offers include travel assistance for an initial six-month period.

The Ostara bakery remains in production while customer orders are transferred in stages. Staff have paid time for interviews and employment advice. Managing director Tessa Oakhill thanked employees for their proposals and said the decision reflects the building's operating costs and low utilisation, rather than the quality of their work.

title: Oakhill Reports Lower Bread Waste Across Its Operating Bakeries
author: Mara Denholt
body:
Oakhill Bakeries Group reduced bread production waste to 2.8 per cent of baked weight in September, down from 3.6 per cent in June. The comparison covers Amberford, Saltmarsh and Ostara, which operated during both months. It excludes the new Kestrel Bay bakery.

The measure includes misshapen loaves, products damaged during packing and bread rejected during quality checks. It does not include unsold goods returned by shops, which Oakhill records separately. Production waste across the three sites fell from 54 tonnes in June to 43 tonnes in September.

Teams adjusted dough portion settings, improved checks at shift changes and replaced worn guides on two packing lines. Operations director Brenna Halewick said these small changes reduced avoidable losses without relaxing product standards. Site teams review the figures weekly, using weighing records and production totals to identify where further checks are needed.

title: Val-Brume Customers Receive Updated French Language Product Information
author: Lucien Bréval
body:
Oakhill Bakeries Group has issued updated French language product sheets for customers in Val-Brume and the surrounding French-speaking region. The sheets cover 34 products and bring ingredients, allergens, pack sizes and storage instructions into one consistent format for shop staff and catering teams.

The update follows customer feedback that older documents used different layouts and made pack sizes difficult to find. Each sheet now includes a product code, revision date and a clear statement of the number of items in a case. Recipes and wholesale prices are unchanged.

Printed copies are available through delivery drivers, alongside electronic versions from the customer service team. French-speaking staff checked the wording against current production specifications. Commercial manager Nerys Fennholt said the clearer information helps customers answer routine questions at the counter and identify the correct product when placing or checking an order.

title: Ostara Bakery Ends Production as Staff Transfers Take Effect
author: Elin Veymar
body:
Production has ended at Oakhill Bakeries Group's Ostara bakery. The final shift completed its orders yesterday, and the site is closed for baking from today. Customer orders have been transferred to Amberford and Kestrel Bay, with no changes to agreed delivery days.

Of the 31 employees affected, 19 have transferred within the group and 12 have left through redundancy. Transferring staff include 11 colleagues joining Amberford and eight already working at Kestrel Bay. All departing employees have received written confirmation of their final pay and redundancy arrangements.

A small facilities team is securing the building and recording equipment for removal or reuse. No decision has been made about the property's longer-term use. Managing director Tessa Oakhill thanked the Ostara team for completing the final orders carefully and supporting colleagues during the transfer of products and production records.

title: Oakhill Revises Wholesale Prices Following Flour Cost Increases
author: Lucien Bréval
body:

The wholesale price of a standard 800g white loaf has risen from KRN 4.10 to KRN 4.23. A pack of six plain rolls has increased from KRN 3.60 to KRN 3.72. Prices for seven products, including selected sweet buns, remain unchanged.

Commercial manager Nerys Fennholt said savings from production and purchasing have absorbed part of the rise.
